docs.title: Why vector databases, and why now
docs.text: Every retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system, semantic search feature, and recommendation engine shipping today leans on the same underlying idea: turn content into vectors, then find the nearest ones fast. That's a different problem from anything a traditional database was built to solve efficiently at scale — which is why a whole category of purpose-built vector databases (Pinecone, Weaviate, Qdrant) and vector-native extensions (pgvector) has emerged. This course treats that as its own discipline: how embeddings actually work, how approximate nearest-neighbor search makes billion-vector queries return in milliseconds, and how to run all of it reliably in production.

docs.title: 01 · What Are Embeddings & Why Vector Search
The problem with keyword search
docs.text:
Classic search (grep, SQL LIKE, full-text indexes) matches on words. That breaks the moment two pieces of text mean the same thing but say it differently:

  • "My laptop won't turn on" vs. "device fails to power up" — zero shared keywords, same problem.
  • "Apple released a new phone" vs. "apple pie recipe" — shares the word "apple", completely different topics.

Keyword matching can't tell these apart because it never represents meaning — only strings.

docs.title: What an embedding actually is
docs.text:
An embedding is a fixed-length list of numbers (a vector) produced by a model that has learned to place semantically similar inputs close together and dissimilar inputs far apart. For text, a sentence like "a sleepy cat" might become something like:

[0.12, -0.44, 0.08, ..., 0.31]   # e.g. 384 numbers for a small model

The individual numbers mean nothing on their own — you can't point to dimension 57 and say "that's catness." What matters is relative position: vectors for related concepts cluster together in this high-dimensional space.

docs.title: A worked example (toy vectors, no model yet)
docs.text:
To build intuition before touching a real embedding model, imagine a pretend 2D "meaning space" where we've hand-placed a few sentences:

import numpy as np

# Pretend embeddings — hand-picked to illustrate the idea, not real output
vectors = {
    "my laptop won't turn on":        np.array([0.9, 0.8]),
    "device fails to power up":       np.array([0.85, 0.75]),   # similar MEANING
    "apple released a new phone":     np.array([-0.6, 0.5]),
    "apple pie recipe":                np.array([-0.5, -0.9]),  # similar WORD, different meaning
}

def euclidean(a, b):
    return np.linalg.norm(a - b)

query = vectors["my laptop won't turn on"]
for text, vec in vectors.items():
    print(f"{text:35s} distance={euclidean(query, vec):.3f}")

my laptop won't turn on            distance=0.000
device fails to power up           distance=0.071
apple released a new phone         distance=1.517
apple pie recipe                   distance=2.102

"device fails to power up" lands almost on top of the laptop complaint — despite sharing no words with it. Meanwhile "apple released a new phone" and "apple pie recipe" share a word but sit far apart from each other, and both sit far from the laptop sentences. That's the whole idea of vector search: distance in embedding space approximates distance in meaning.

docs.title: Why this course exists
docs.text:
Once you can turn any piece of content — a sentence, a paragraph, an image, a product description — into a vector, a huge number of problems reduce to one operation: "find the vectors nearest to this one."

  • Semantic search: embed a user's query, find the nearest document chunks.
  • RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation): embed a question, retrieve the most relevant chunks, hand them to an LLM as context.
  • Recommendations: embed a user's history, find nearby items.
  • Deduplication / clustering: group vectors that sit close together.

A vector database is just a system purpose-built to store millions (or billions) of these vectors and answer "find the nearest ones" queries fast. That's what the rest of this course is about: generating real embeddings, understanding how "nearest" is measured, and running that search at scale using real vector databases.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
Without writing any code, sketch (on paper or in a comment block) three pairs of sentences:

  1. A pair that means the same thing but shares no keywords.
  2. A pair that shares a keyword but means different things.
  3. A pair that is both keyword-similar and meaning-similar.

For each pair, predict whether a keyword search engine and a vector search engine would consider them "similar," and write one sentence explaining why they'd disagree (or agree) in each case. You'll verify these predictions with a real model in Lesson 5.

docs.title: 02 · Setup: Python, NumPy & Your First Vectors
Install Python and NumPy
docs.text:
You'll need Python 3.9+ for this course.

# macOS (Homebrew)
brew install python

# Ubuntu/Debian
sudo apt install python3 python3-pip

# Windows
# Download from https://www.python.org/downloads/

Create a virtual environment and install NumPy:

python3 -m venv venv
source venv/bin/activate      # Windows: venv\Scripts\activate
pip install numpy

Verify it:

import numpy as np
print(np.__version__)

docs.title: Creating your first vectors
docs.text:
A vector in this course is just a 1-dimensional NumPy array of floats:

import numpy as np

v = np.array([0.2, 0.9, -0.1])
print(v)          # [ 0.2  0.9 -0.1]
print(v.shape)     # (3,)
print(v.dtype)     # float64

Real embedding models produce vectors with hundreds of dimensions (384, 768, 1536 are common sizes), but the math is identical whether you have 3 numbers or 1536 — NumPy doesn't care.

docs.title: Basic vector operations
docs.text:
a = np.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0])
b = np.array([4.0, 5.0, 6.0])

a + b              # array([5., 7., 9.])   element-wise addition
a - b              # array([-3., -3., -3.])
a * 2.0            # array([2., 4., 6.])   scalar multiply
a * b              # array([4., 10., 18.]) element-wise multiply (NOT dot product)

docs.title: Magnitude (norm)
docs.text:
The magnitude (or norm, or length) of a vector tells you how far it is from the origin. For a 3D vector [x, y, z] it's the familiar Pythagorean formula extended to N dimensions:

‖v‖ = sqrt(v₁² + v₂² + ... + vₙ²)

v = np.array([3.0, 4.0])
magnitude = np.linalg.norm(v)
print(magnitude)   # 5.0   (3-4-5 right triangle)

np.linalg.norm works for any number of dimensions:

v = np.array([0.2, 0.9, -0.1, 0.4, -0.6])
print(np.linalg.norm(v))   # sqrt(0.04+0.81+0.01+0.16+0.36) ≈ 1.095

You'll use this constantly: normalizing a vector (dividing it by its own magnitude) produces a unit vector — same direction, length exactly 1 — which is the basis for cosine similarity in the next lesson.

def normalize(v):
    return v / np.linalg.norm(v)

unit = normalize(np.array([3.0, 4.0]))
print(unit)                      # [0.6 0.8]
print(np.linalg.norm(unit))      # 1.0

docs.title: Representing toy "documents" as vectors
docs.text:
Before you generate real embeddings in Lesson 5, it helps to hand-craft a tiny dataset so you can reason about the numbers directly. Imagine a 4-dimensional space where each dimension loosely tracks a theme — [animals, technology, food, sports]:

documents = {
    "doc1": np.array([0.9, 0.1, 0.0, 0.0]),   # about animals
    "doc2": np.array([0.8, 0.2, 0.1, 0.0]),   # also about animals, slightly tech
    "doc3": np.array([0.0, 0.9, 0.1, 0.0]),   # about technology
    "doc4": np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.1, 0.9]),   # about sports
}

for name, vec in documents.items():
    print(name, "magnitude:", round(np.linalg.norm(vec), 3))

Real models never hand you interpretable dimensions like this — but keeping this toy dataset around for the next two lessons will let you verify that your distance and similarity code behaves the way you expect before you point it at opaque, 384-number real embeddings.

docs.title: 03 · Distance Metrics (Cosine, Euclidean, Dot Product)
docs.text: Every vector search boils down to "how far apart are these two vectors?" — but "far apart" can mean different things. This lesson covers the three metrics you'll see in every vector database you touch.

docs.title: Euclidean distance (L2)
docs.text:
Straight-line distance between two points, generalized to N dimensions:

import numpy as np

def euclidean_distance(a, b):
    return np.linalg.norm(a - b)

a = np.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0])
b = np.array([2.0, 1.0, 4.0])
print(euclidean_distance(a, b))   # sqrt(1+1+1) ≈ 1.732

Euclidean distance cares about absolute position, including magnitude. Two vectors pointing in the exact same direction but with different lengths will have nonzero Euclidean distance between them.

docs.title: Dot product
docs.text:
def dot_product(a, b):
    return np.dot(a, b)

print(dot_product(a, b))   # 1*2 + 2*1 + 3*4 = 16

The dot product gets larger as vectors point in more similar directions and have larger magnitudes — it's a similarity measure, not a distance (bigger = more similar, unlike the distances above where smaller = more similar).

docs.title: Cosine similarity
docs.text:
Cosine similarity measures the angle between two vectors, ignoring their magnitude entirely:

def cosine_similarity(a, b):
    return np.dot(a, b) / (np.linalg.norm(a) * np.linalg.norm(b))

a = np.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0])
b = np.array([2.0, 4.0, 6.0])   # same direction as a, just scaled 2x
print(cosine_similarity(a, b))   # 1.0 — identical direction, "perfectly similar"
print(euclidean_distance(a, b))  # 3.74 — but far apart in Euclidean terms!

This is why cosine is the default for text embeddings: two embeddings for "I love this product" and "I LOVE THIS PRODUCT!!!" might differ in magnitude (different word counts, different emphasis) but should still be judged as pointing in nearly the same semantic direction.

Cosine similarity ranges from -1 (opposite) through 0 (unrelated/ orthogonal) to 1 (identical direction).

docs.title: When to use which
docs.text:
Metric Use when... Cosine Default for text embeddings — direction (meaning) matters, magnitude doesn't Euclidean Absolute position matters — e.g. spatial coordinates, some image embeddings Dot product You've already normalized every vector to unit length — then it equals cosine, but is cheaper to compute

Every vector database you'll use in this course (Chroma, Pinecone, Weaviate, Qdrant, pgvector) lets you pick a metric per collection/index — usually cosine, l2 (Euclidean), or dotproduct/ip (inner product).

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Why does normalizing a vector make dot product behave exactly like cosine similarity?

  1. Cosine similarity's formula is (a · b) / (‖a‖ ‖b‖). It's the dot product, scaled down by both vectors' magnitudes.
  2. If both vectors are already unit length (‖a‖ = 1 and ‖b‖ = 1), the denominator becomes 1 * 1 = 1, so the formula collapses to just a · b — the raw dot product.
  3. This means: normalize once, compare cheaply forever. A production vector database can normalize every embedding exactly once at insert time, then use the plain dot product (a single fused multiply-add loop, extremely cheap on modern CPUs/GPUs with SIMD instructions) for every future comparison — instead of recomputing two norm() calls on every single query-to-vector comparison.
  4. This is why most embedding models (including sentence-transformers models you'll use in Lesson 5) ship with a normalize_embeddings=True option — so you can store unit vectors and let the database use the fastest possible similarity operation while still getting cosine semantics.
  5. Verify it yourself:
def normalize(v):
    return v / np.linalg.norm(v)

a = np.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0])
b = np.array([2.0, 1.0, 4.0])

cos_sim = cosine_similarity(a, b)
dot_of_normalized = np.dot(normalize(a), normalize(b))

print(cos_sim, dot_of_normalized)   # same value, two different routes

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Using the 4 toy documents from Lesson 2 (documents dict with [animals, technology, food, sports] dimensions), write a function that computes the cosine similarity of doc1 against doc2, doc3, and doc4. Print the results sorted from most to least similar, and in a one-line comment explain whether the ranking matches what you'd intuitively expect given the documents' themes.

docs.title: The simplest possible vector search
docs.text:
Before touching a real database, build the search algorithm every vector database is secretly approximating under the hood: compare your query against every stored vector, and return the closest ones.

import numpy as np

documents = {
    "doc1": np.array([0.9, 0.1, 0.0, 0.0]),
    "doc2": np.array([0.8, 0.2, 0.1, 0.0]),
    "doc3": np.array([0.0, 0.9, 0.1, 0.0]),
    "doc4": np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.1, 0.9]),
    "doc5": np.array([0.85, 0.15, 0.05, 0.0]),
}

def cosine_similarity(a, b):
    return np.dot(a, b) / (np.linalg.norm(a) * np.linalg.norm(b))

def brute_force_search(query, documents, top_k=3):
    scored = [
        (name, cosine_similarity(query, vec))
        for name, vec in documents.items()
    ]
    scored.sort(key=lambda pair: pair[1], reverse=True)
    return scored[:top_k]

query = np.array([0.88, 0.12, 0.0, 0.0])   # "about animals"
results = brute_force_search(query, documents, top_k=3)
for name, score in results:
    print(f"{name}: {score:.4f}")

doc5: 0.9999
doc1: 0.9937
doc2: 0.9802

That's it — this is a real, correct nearest-neighbor search. Every vector database's job is ultimately to return exactly this ranking, just faster.

docs.title: Scaling it up with pure NumPy
docs.text:
For a slightly larger, more realistic dataset, do it in one vectorized pass instead of a Python loop — this is how you'd actually write it outside a toy example:

import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=42)
n_docs, dims = 10_000, 128

# Simulate 10,000 random "document" vectors
dataset = rng.normal(size=(n_docs, dims))
dataset = dataset / np.linalg.norm(dataset, axis=1, keepdims=True)  # normalize each row

query = rng.normal(size=(dims,))
query = query / np.linalg.norm(query)

# One matrix-vector multiply computes similarity to ALL 10,000 vectors at once
similarities = dataset @ query          # shape (10000,)
top_k = 5
top_indices = np.argsort(similarities)[::-1][:top_k]

for idx in top_indices:
    print(f"doc #{idx}: similarity={similarities[idx]:.4f}")

Because every vector is pre-normalized, dataset @ query is a single dot product per row — cosine similarity computed for all 10,000 documents in one NumPy call.

docs.title: Timing it
docs.text:
import time

start = time.perf_counter()
similarities = dataset @ query
elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start
print(f"Searched {n_docs} vectors in {elapsed*1000:.2f} ms")

On a laptop, 10,000 128-dimensional vectors search in a few milliseconds. Feels instant. The problem starts when n_docs grows.

docs.title: Why this doesn't scale
docs.text:
Brute force is O(n): double the number of vectors, double the search time, no exceptions. That's fine at 10,000 vectors. It stops being fine at real-world scale:

Dataset size Rough brute-force search time* 10,000 vectors ~1-5 ms 1,000,000 vectors ~100-500 ms 100,000,000 vectors ~10-50 seconds 1,000,000,000 vectors minutes

*Rough order-of-magnitude, single machine, single query — actual numbers depend on dimensionality and hardware.

A production RAG system or recommendation engine needs to answer queries in tens of milliseconds, against collections that can hold hundreds of millions to billions of vectors, often with many queries per second concurrently. Linear scan simply cannot keep up — you can't compute a billion dot products per query, per second, no matter how fast your CPU is.

This is exactly the gap that Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) search fills — trading a small amount of accuracy for a massive speedup by not checking every vector. You'll get your first real taste of how in Lesson 6, and the full mechanics (HNSW, IVF, product quantization) in Level 2.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Extend the timing experiment above: run the same brute-force search at n_docs = 1_000, 10_000, 100_000, and 1_000_000 (keep dims = 128), timing each with time.perf_counter(). Plot or print the results and confirm the relationship between n_docs and search time is roughly linear, as the O(n) label predicts.

docs.title: 05 · Generating Real Embeddings
docs.text: So far every vector has been hand-crafted. Time to generate real ones from real text using a real, open-source embedding model.

docs.title: Install sentence-transformers
docs.text:
pip install sentence-transformers

This pulls in PyTorch and Hugging Face's transformers library under the hood — the first import may take a few seconds while it loads.

docs.title: Load a model and encode a sentence
docs.text:
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer

model = SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2")

embedding = model.encode("My laptop won't turn on")
print(embedding.shape)   # (384,)
print(embedding[:5])     # first 5 of 384 numbers

The first call downloads the model (~90MB) from Hugging Face and caches it locally (~/.cache/huggingface by default) — subsequent runs load instantly from disk, no network required.

all-MiniLM-L6-v2 is a good default for this course: small (fast on CPU, no GPU needed), well-tested, and produces 384-dimensional embeddings that are normalized to work well with cosine similarity.

docs.title: Encoding many sentences at once
docs.text:
sentences = [
    "My laptop won't turn on",
    "Device fails to power up",
    "Apple released a new phone",
    "Apple pie recipe with cinnamon",
]

embeddings = model.encode(sentences)
print(embeddings.shape)   # (4, 384) — 4 sentences, 384 dims each

Batching like this (passing a list instead of calling .encode() in a loop) is significantly faster — the model processes all sentences together.

docs.title: Revisiting Lesson 1's prediction with real numbers
docs.text:
Lesson 1 predicted that "my laptop won't turn on" and "device fails to power up" would land close together despite sharing no words, while "apple released a new phone" and "apple pie recipe" would land far apart despite sharing a word. Now you can check that with a real model:

import numpy as np

def cosine_similarity(a, b):
    return np.dot(a, b) / (np.linalg.norm(a) * np.linalg.norm(b))

laptop_vec = embeddings[0]
device_vec = embeddings[1]
iphone_vec = embeddings[2]
pie_vec = embeddings[3]

print("laptop vs device (different words, same meaning):",
      cosine_similarity(laptop_vec, device_vec))
print("iphone vs pie (shared word 'apple', different meaning):",
      cosine_similarity(iphone_vec, pie_vec))

laptop vs device (different words, same meaning):  0.63
iphone vs pie (shared word 'apple', different meaning):  0.18

Exact numbers vary by model version, but the pattern holds: the meaning-similar pair scores noticeably higher than the keyword-similar, meaning-different pair. This is the real version of the toy example from Lesson 1 — no hand-picked vectors, just a model that learned this structure from training on billions of real sentences.

docs.title: Running Lesson 4's brute-force search on real embeddings
docs.text:
Now plug real embeddings into the brute-force search you already wrote:

corpus = [
    "The cat sat on the windowsill watching birds.",
    "Our server crashed during the deployment last night.",
    "She baked a chocolate cake for the party.",
    "The kitten chased a laser pointer across the floor.",
    "We rolled back the release after it broke production.",
]

corpus_embeddings = model.encode(corpus)
query = "the website went down after we shipped new code"
query_embedding = model.encode(query)

def brute_force_search(query_vec, corpus_vecs, corpus_texts, top_k=3):
    scores = [cosine_similarity(query_vec, vec) for vec in corpus_vecs]
    ranked = sorted(zip(corpus_texts, scores), key=lambda p: p[1], reverse=True)
    return ranked[:top_k]

for text, score in brute_force_search(query_embedding, corpus_embeddings, corpus):
    print(f"{score:.3f}  {text}")

You should see the deployment/rollback sentences rank highest — despite the query sharing almost no exact words with either of them.

Encode them all with model.encode(), then write 3 test queries — one per topic — and print the top-3 brute-force results for each. Confirm the model groups each query with sentences from the matching topic, not the other two.

docs.title: 06 · Intro to Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search
The core trade-off
docs.text:
Lesson 4 showed that brute-force search is O(n) — every query has to touch every vector. Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) search breaks that rule on purpose: it pre-organizes vectors into a data structure that lets a query skip over most of the dataset, at the cost of occasionally missing the true single best match in exchange for something nearly as good, much faster.

"Approximate" sounds risky, but in practice a well-tuned ANN index finds the true top-k results (or something essentially as relevant) 95-99%+ of the time — a trade nearly every production system is happy to make for a 10-100x speedup.

docs.title: Why organization beats brute checking
docs.text:
Think about how you'd find a word in a dictionary. You don't read every page — you flip to roughly the right letter, then narrow down. That's only possible because the dictionary is organized (alphabetically). Unorganized data forces a linear scan; organized data lets you skip straight to the relevant region.

ANN indexes do the same thing for vector space: they build a structure at insert time so that at query time, you can jump straight to the neighborhood that's likely to contain the nearest vectors, instead of visiting every single one.

docs.title: A quick taste: clustering as a crude ANN
docs.text:
One of the simplest ANN ideas — group vectors into clusters, and at query time only search the clusters nearest the query, not all of them:

import numpy as np
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans   # pip install scikit-learn

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
dataset = rng.normal(size=(10_000, 64))
dataset /= np.linalg.norm(dataset, axis=1, keepdims=True)

# Partition into 50 clusters at "index build" time
kmeans = KMeans(n_clusters=50, random_state=0).fit(dataset)
cluster_centers = kmeans.cluster_centers_
cluster_labels = kmeans.labels_

def ann_cluster_search(query, top_clusters=3, top_k=5):
    # Step 1: find the nearest cluster centers (fast — only 50 comparisons)
    center_sims = cluster_centers @ query
    nearest_clusters = np.argsort(center_sims)[::-1][:top_clusters]

    # Step 2: only brute-force search WITHIN those clusters
    candidate_mask = np.isin(cluster_labels, nearest_clusters)
    candidates = dataset[candidate_mask]
    candidate_indices = np.where(candidate_mask)[0]

    sims = candidates @ query
    top = np.argsort(sims)[::-1][:top_k]
    return candidate_indices[top], sims[top]

query = rng.normal(size=(64,))
query /= np.linalg.norm(query)

indices, scores = ann_cluster_search(query)
print(list(zip(indices, scores)))

Instead of 10,000 comparisons, this does roughly 50 + (10,000/50 * 3) ≈ 650 — about 15x fewer comparisons, at the cost of occasionally missing a true nearest neighbor that happened to fall just outside the 3 clusters searched. (This exact technique, done properly, is called IVF — Inverted File Index — and you'll build it for real in Level 2, Lesson 6.)

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Real production ANN indexes (like HNSW — Hierarchical Navigable Small World graphs, used by Chroma, Pinecone, Weaviate, Qdrant, and pgvector) take this idea much further. You'll implement and tune HNSW in depth in Level 2, Lesson 5 — but the intuition is worth building now:

  1. Vectors become nodes in a graph, connected to a handful of their nearest neighbors — not to everything, just a small set of "close friends."
  2. The graph has multiple layers, like a highway system. The top layer has very few nodes with long-range connections (the highways); lower layers have progressively more nodes with short-range connections (the side streets).
  3. A query starts at the top layer and greedily moves toward whichever connected node is closest to the query — covering large distances in very few hops, the same way you'd take a highway before exiting onto local roads.
  4. It drops down a layer each time it stops improving, repeating the greedy walk on a denser layer, until it's walked all the way down to the bottom (densest) layer and converged on a small set of very close candidates.
  5. Total comparisons per query end up roughly logarithmic in dataset size (O(log n)) instead of linear (O(n)) — which is why HNSW search on a billion vectors can still return results in single-digit milliseconds, something no brute-force approach could ever do.
  6. The "approximate" part: because the walk is greedy (always move toward the locally-closest neighbor) rather than exhaustive, it can get stuck in a locally-good-but-not-globally-best region — missing the true best match in a small fraction of queries. Tuning parameters (search width, number of layers) let you trade recall for speed.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Modify the clustering example above to measure recall: run ann_cluster_search for 50 random queries, and for each one also run true brute-force search (dataset @ query, full sort) to get the real top-5. Compute what fraction of the ANN result's top-5 indices actually appear in the true top-5. Then re-run with top_clusters=1 and top_clusters=10 and observe how recall changes as you search more (or fewer) clusters.

docs.title: 07 · Your First Vector DB: Chroma
docs.text: Everything so far has lived in plain Python lists and NumPy arrays. Time to use an actual vector database — Chroma, a free, open-source, embedded vector database that runs in-process (no server to stand up), making it the easiest place to start.

docs.title: Install Chroma
docs.text: pip install chromadb

docs.title: Create a persistent client
docs.text:
import chromadb

client = chromadb.PersistentClient(path="./chroma_data")

PersistentClient writes to disk at the given path, so your data survives between runs. (There's also chromadb.Client() for a purely in-memory instance that disappears when the process exits — fine for quick experiments, not for anything you want to keep.)

docs.title: Create a collection
docs.text:
A collection in Chroma is roughly the equivalent of a table — a named group of vectors plus their metadata and original text.

collection = client.get_or_create_collection(name="my_first_collection")

get_or_create_collection is idiomatic here — it creates the collection the first time you run your script and reuses it on every subsequent run, instead of erroring out on "already exists."

docs.title: Adding documents
docs.text:
Chroma can embed text for you automatically — pass documents (raw text) and it uses a built-in default embedding model behind the scenes, no manual model.encode() call required:

collection.add(
    ids=["doc1", "doc2", "doc3", "doc4"],
    documents=[
        "The cat sat on the windowsill watching birds.",
        "Our server crashed during the deployment last night.",
        "She baked a chocolate cake for the party.",
        "The kitten chased a laser pointer across the floor.",
    ],
)

Chroma's default embedding function downloads a small sentence-transformers model the first time you call .add() — similar to what you used directly in Lesson 5.

docs.title: Using your own embeddings instead
docs.text:
If you'd rather control embedding generation yourself (e.g. to reuse the exact model from Lesson 5, or a different one later in this course), pass embeddings directly instead of letting Chroma compute them:

from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer

model = SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2")
texts = [
    "The cat sat on the windowsill watching birds.",
    "Our server crashed during the deployment last night.",
]
vectors = model.encode(texts).tolist()   # Chroma wants plain Python lists

collection.add(
    ids=["doc1", "doc2"],
    documents=texts,
    embeddings=vectors,
)

Either approach works — this course will mostly let Chroma auto-embed for simplicity, and switch to manual embeddings when a lesson needs a specific model.

docs.title: Querying
docs.text:
results = collection.query(
    query_texts=["the website went down after we shipped new code"],
    n_results=2,
)

for doc, distance in zip(results["documents"][0], results["distances"][0]):
    print(f"{distance:.4f}  {doc}")

0.6123  Our server crashed during the deployment last night.
1.1872  The cat sat on the windowsill watching birds.

Notice query_texts (not query_embeddings) — Chroma embeds your query text with the same embedding function it used for .add(), so you never have to manually embed a query when you're letting Chroma handle embedding.

docs.title: Putting it together
docs.text:
import chromadb

client = chromadb.PersistentClient(path="./chroma_data")
collection = client.get_or_create_collection(name="my_first_collection")

if collection.count() == 0:
    collection.add(
        ids=["doc1", "doc2", "doc3", "doc4"],
        documents=[
            "The cat sat on the windowsill watching birds.",
            "Our server crashed during the deployment last night.",
            "She baked a chocolate cake for the party.",
            "The kitten chased a laser pointer across the floor.",
        ],
    )

results = collection.query(query_texts=["pets playing"], n_results=2)
print(results["documents"][0])

The collection.count() == 0 check keeps this script idempotent — run it twice and you won't get duplicate-ID errors from calling .add() again on data that's already there.

Write three different queries — one that should clearly match each topic — and print the top-2 results for each, confirming they come from the expected topic group.

docs.title: 08 · Indexing & Querying Basics
docs.text: With the fundamentals from Lesson 7 in place, this lesson goes one level deeper into the Chroma operations you'll use in nearly every real project: controlling result count, reading back similarity scores, updating and deleting entries, and confirming your data really does persist.

docs.title: Controlling how many results come back
docs.text:
n_results (sometimes called top_k in other databases) controls how many matches you get per query:

results = collection.query(
    query_texts=["production incident"],
    n_results=5,     # default is 10 if you omit it
)

You can also query with multiple texts in one call — Chroma returns one result set per query, batched:

results = collection.query(
    query_texts=["production incident", "something about pets"],
    n_results=3,
)

for i, query_text in enumerate(["production incident", "something about pets"]):
    print(f"\nResults for: {query_text}")
    for doc, dist in zip(results["documents"][i], results["distances"][i]):
        print(f"  {dist:.4f}  {doc}")

docs.title: Reading distances and understanding the scale
docs.text:
Chroma's default distance metric is squared Euclidean (l2) unless you configure the collection otherwise. Lower distance = more similar — the opposite direction from cosine similarity, where higher means more similar. Don't mix these up when sorting results manually.

You can set the distance metric explicitly at collection creation:

collection = client.get_or_create_collection(
    name="my_collection",
    metadata={"hnsw:space": "cosine"},   # options: "l2", "cosine", "ip"
)

Chroma uses an HNSW index under the hood (the same algorithm you got an intuition for in Lesson 6) — hnsw:space controls which distance function that index is built around.

docs.title: Updating entries
docs.text:
collection.update(
    ids=["doc1"],
    documents=["The cat sat on the windowsill, intently watching two birds."],
)

update() requires the ids to already exist. To insert-or-replace in one call regardless of whether the id exists yet, use upsert() instead:

collection.upsert(
    ids=["doc5"],
    documents=["A new document that may or may not already exist."],
)

docs.title: Deleting entries
docs.text:
collection.delete(ids=["doc3"])

# Or delete everything matching a metadata filter (covered fully in Lesson 9):
collection.delete(where={"category": "spam"})

docs.title: Checking what's in a collection
docs.text:
print(collection.count())          # how many items are stored

peek = collection.peek(limit=3)     # sample a few items without a real query
print(peek["ids"])

docs.title: Verifying persistence across restarts
docs.text:
Because PersistentClient writes to disk, you can close your Python process entirely and reopen the same data later — this is the entire point of using a persistent client instead of the in-memory one:

# Run 1 — insert data, then exit the process entirely
import chromadb
client = chromadb.PersistentClient(path="./chroma_data")
collection = client.get_or_create_collection(name="persisted_demo")
collection.add(ids=["a"], documents=["This should still be here next time."])
print("inserted, count =", collection.count())

# Run 2 — a completely fresh process, pointed at the same path
import chromadb
client = chromadb.PersistentClient(path="./chroma_data")
collection = client.get_or_create_collection(name="persisted_demo")
print("count after reopening:", collection.count())   # 1 — nothing lost
print(collection.get(ids=["a"]))

No explicit "save" call is needed — Chroma writes to the on-disk path as you go. This matters because in any real application, your ingestion script and your query-serving process (e.g. a web API) are usually separate Python processes, sometimes on separate deploys — they only share data because they point at the same persistent path.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Starting from the my_notes collection you built in Lesson 7's exercise: update one document's text, upsert one brand-new document, delete one document you no longer want, and confirm the final collection.count() matches what you expect by hand. Then close your Python session completely, reopen it, reconnect to the same PersistentClient path, and verify the collection still contains exactly those changes.

docs.title: 09 · Metadata Filtering
docs.text: Pure vector similarity answers "what's semantically closest?" but real applications usually need to combine that with hard constraints: only search this user's documents, only this category, only documents newer than a given date. That's what metadata filtering is for.

docs.title: Attaching metadata on insert
docs.text:
import chromadb

client = chromadb.PersistentClient(path="./chroma_data")
collection = client.get_or_create_collection(name="support_tickets")

collection.add(
    ids=["t1", "t2", "t3", "t4"],
    documents=[
        "Customer can't log in after password reset.",
        "Invoice total looks wrong for last month's subscription.",
        "App crashes when uploading a profile photo.",
        "Refund requested for duplicate charge on credit card.",
    ],
    metadatas=[
        {"category": "auth", "year": 2024, "priority": "high"},
        {"category": "billing", "year": 2024, "priority": "medium"},
        {"category": "bug", "year": 2023, "priority": "high"},
        {"category": "billing", "year": 2024, "priority": "high"},
    ],
)

Each item in metadatas must line up positionally with the matching id in ids — Chroma stores them together.

docs.title: Filtering with where
docs.text:
results = collection.query(
    query_texts=["money was charged twice"],
    n_results=5,
    where={"category": "billing"},
)

for doc, meta, dist in zip(
    results["documents"][0], results["metadatas"][0], results["distances"][0]
):
    print(f"{dist:.4f}  {meta}  {doc}")

This only ranks and returns documents where category == "billing" — vector similarity still determines the order within that filtered set, but anything outside the filter is excluded entirely before ranking happens.

docs.title: Combining multiple conditions
docs.text:
# Billing issues from 2024 only
results = collection.query(
    query_texts=["money was charged twice"],
    n_results=5,
    where={
        "$and": [
            {"category": "billing"},
            {"year": 2024},
        ]
    },
)

Chroma supports comparison operators too:

# High priority items only
where={"priority": {"$eq": "high"}}

# Anything from 2024 or later
where={"year": {"$gte": 2024}}

# Either billing OR auth category
where={"$or": [{"category": "billing"}, {"category": "auth"}]}

docs.title: Filtering on document text itself
docs.text:
Separate from metadata filtering, where_document filters on substring matches in the raw document text, and can be combined with where:

results = collection.query(
    query_texts=["login problem"],
    n_results=5,
    where={"year": 2024},
    where_document={"$contains": "password"},
)

docs.title: Deleting by metadata filter
docs.text:
Filters aren't just for queries — they also work with .delete(), useful for bulk cleanup:

# Remove every low-priority item from 2023
collection.delete(where={"$and": [{"priority": "low"}, {"year": 2023}]})

docs.title: Why this matters for real systems
docs.text:
Almost every production use of vector search needs this. A few concrete examples:

  • Multi-tenant SaaS: where={"customer_id": current_customer.id} so one customer's semantic search never surfaces another customer's documents.
  • RAG over a knowledge base with access control: where={"visibility": "public"} or where={"team": current_user.team}.
  • Time-scoped search: "find similar support tickets, but only from the last 90 days" — combine a date filter with the similarity query.

Without metadata filtering, you'd have to run the vector query first, over-fetch a huge number of results, then filter in application code — wasteful and error-prone. Filtering during the query itself is both faster and correct by construction.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
Extend the support_tickets collection with 6 more tickets covering at least 3 categories, 2 different years, and a mix of priorities. Write three queries:

  1. A semantic query combined with a single metadata filter.
  2. A semantic query combined with an $and of two metadata conditions.
  3. A semantic query combined with an $or across two categories.

For each, print the results and manually verify every returned item actually satisfies the filter you specified.

docs.title: 10 · Project — Semantic Search CLI
docs.text: Time to combine everything from this level into one working tool: a command-line semantic search engine over your own text files.

docs.title: What you're building
docs.text:
A CLI with two commands:

# 1. Index every .txt file in a folder
python search_cli.py index ./my_notes

# 2. Search across everything you've indexed
python search_cli.py search "how do I reset my vpn connection"

Example expected output for search:

$ python search_cli.py search "how do I reset my vpn connection"

1. [0.847] notes/it-setup.txt
   "...if the VPN client won't connect, try restarting the adapter
   and re-entering your credentials before escalating to IT..."

2. [0.621] notes/onboarding.txt
   "...network access requires connecting through the company VPN,
   which you'll set up during your first week..."

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
1. index <folder> walks a folder, reads every .txt file, splits each file into chunks (don't embed a whole file as one vector — see "Why chunking matters" below), embeds each chunk with sentence-transformers, and stores them in a persistent Chroma collection with metadata recording which file (and roughly which position in it) each chunk came from.
  2. search <query> embeds the query, runs it against the persisted collection, and prints the top-5 results: similarity score, source filename, and a snippet of the matching chunk.
  3. Running index twice on the same folder should not duplicate entries (reuse Lesson 8's upsert or clear-and-rebuild, your choice — just avoid silent duplicates).
  4. Use Python's argparse or sys.argv to make this a real CLI, not just two separate scripts.

docs.title: Why chunking matters
docs.text: If you embed an entire 2,000-word file as a single vector, that vector ends up representing the average meaning of the whole file — a single paragraph about VPN setup buried inside a much longer onboarding document gets diluted into near-meaninglessness. Splitting a file into smaller chunks (e.g. every ~3-5 sentences, or every paragraph) before embedding means each chunk's vector represents one coherent idea, and your search can point directly at the relevant paragraph instead of just "somewhere in this file." You'll go much deeper on chunking strategy in Level 3, Lesson 3 — for this project, a simple paragraph-or-fixed-size split is enough.

docs.title: Suggested structure
docs.text:
# search_cli.py
import argparse
import pathlib
import chromadb
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer

MODEL_NAME = "all-MiniLM-L6-v2"
DB_PATH = "./search_cli_data"
COLLECTION_NAME = "notes"
CHUNK_SIZE = 500   # characters; tune as you like

model = SentenceTransformer(MODEL_NAME)
client = chromadb.PersistentClient(path=DB_PATH)


def chunk_text(text, chunk_size=CHUNK_SIZE):
    """Split text into roughly chunk_size-character pieces, breaking on
    paragraph boundaries where possible."""
    # Your implementation — paragraphs first, then fall back to a hard
    # character split for any paragraph longer than chunk_size.
    ...


def cmd_index(folder):
    collection = client.get_or_create_collection(name=COLLECTION_NAME)
    txt_files = pathlib.Path(folder).glob("**/*.txt")

    for file_path in txt_files:
        text = file_path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
        chunks = chunk_text(text)
        embeddings = model.encode(chunks).tolist()

        ids = [f"{file_path}::{i}" for i in range(len(chunks))]
        metadatas = [{"source": str(file_path), "chunk_index": i} for i in range(len(chunks))]

        collection.upsert(
            ids=ids,
            documents=chunks,
            embeddings=embeddings,
            metadatas=metadatas,
        )
    print(f"Indexed {sum(1 for _ in pathlib.Path(folder).glob('**/*.txt'))} files.")


def cmd_search(query, top_k=5):
    collection = client.get_or_create_collection(name=COLLECTION_NAME)
    query_embedding = model.encode(query).tolist()

    results = collection.query(query_embeddings=[query_embedding], n_results=top_k)

    for rank, (doc, meta, distance) in enumerate(
        zip(results["documents"][0], results["metadatas"][0], results["distances"][0]), start=1
    ):
        similarity = 1 - distance   # rough conversion if using l2; adjust for your metric
        snippet = doc[:200].replace("\n", " ")
        print(f"\n{rank}. [{similarity:.3f}] {meta['source']}")
        print(f'   "...{snippet}..."')


def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Semantic search over local .txt files")
    subparsers = parser.add_subparsers(dest="command", required=True)

    index_parser = subparsers.add_parser("index")
    index_parser.add_argument("folder")

    search_parser = subparsers.add_parser("search")
    search_parser.add_argument("query")

    args = parser.parse_args()

    if args.command == "index":
        cmd_index(args.folder)
    elif args.command == "search":
        cmd_search(args.query)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

The chunk_text() function and the exact similarity-score conversion in cmd_search are left for you to finish — that's the part of this project that's genuinely yours to design.

docs.title: Level 2 · Intermediate Production DBs
docs.text: Goal: move past toy examples and get hands-on with the vector databases teams actually run in production — managed and self-hosted — plus the indexing theory behind why they're fast.

docs.title: Modules
docs.text:
1. Pinecone Fundamentals
  2. Weaviate: Schemas & Hybrid Search
  3. Qdrant: Collections & Payloads
  4. pgvector: Vectors Inside PostgreSQL
  5. How HNSW Actually Works
  6. IVF & Product Quantization

By the end of this level you'll be fluent in four real vector databases, understand the index algorithms that make billion-vector search fast, and have built a retrieval service that pulls from multiple data sources.

docs.title: 01 · Pinecone Fundamentals
docs.text: Pinecone is a fully managed vector database: you never choose an index algorithm, size a cluster, or tune ef_search. You create an index, upsert vectors, and query. That simplicity is the entire value proposition — and the entire lesson.

docs.title: Getting an API key
docs.text:
Sign up at pinecone.io and grab an API key from the console. Store it as an environment variable rather than hardcoding it:

export PINECONE_API_KEY="your-key-here"
pip install pinecone

docs.title: Creating a serverless index
docs.text:
import os
from pinecone import Pinecone, ServerlessSpec

pc = Pinecone(api_key=os.environ["PINECONE_API_KEY"])

pc.create_index(
    name="docs-index",
    dimension=384,  # must match your embedding model's output size
    metric="cosine",
    spec=ServerlessSpec(cloud="aws", region="us-east-1"),
)

index = pc.Index("docs-index")

dimension and metric are fixed at creation time — you can't change them later without recreating the index. 384 matches all-MiniLM-L6-v2 from Level 1; if you switch embedding models, you need a new index.

docs.title: Upserting vectors with metadata
docs.text:
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer

model = SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2")

docs = [
    {"id": "doc-1", "text": "Pinecone is a managed vector database.", "category": "intro"},
    {"id": "doc-2", "text": "HNSW graphs enable fast approximate search.", "category": "internals"},
]

vectors = []
for doc in docs:
    embedding = model.encode(doc["text"]).tolist()
    vectors.append({
        "id": doc["id"],
        "values": embedding,
        "metadata": {"text": doc["text"], "category": doc["category"]},
    })

index.upsert(vectors=vectors)

"Upsert" means insert-or-update: if doc-1 already exists, this overwrites it. There's no separate "insert" call — every write is idempotent by ID.

docs.title: Querying
docs.text:
query_text = "How does managed infrastructure help with vector search?"
query_vector = model.encode(query_text).tolist()

results = index.query(
    vector=query_vector,
    top_k=3,
    include_metadata=True,
)

for match in results["matches"]:
    print(match["score"], match["metadata"]["text"])

score for a cosine-metric index is a similarity in [-1, 1] (higher is better) — note this is the opposite direction from a distance, which is worth checking per provider since not all vector DBs report scores the same way.

docs.title: Why managed infrastructure matters
docs.text: Running your own HNSW cluster means capacity planning: how much RAM for the graph, how many replicas for availability, how to reshard when you outgrow one machine. Pinecone's serverless tier handles all of that behind the API — storage and query throughput scale independently, and you're billed per read/write unit and per GB stored rather than per provisioned node. The tradeoff is less control: you can't inspect or tune the underlying index structure the way you can with a self-hosted database (that's Levels 2.5-2.6, coming next with HNSW and IVF+PQ internals).

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Create a Pinecone index with dimension=384 and metric="cosine", upsert the 10 file summaries from your Level 1 semantic search CLI project (reuse the embeddings you already computed with sentence-transformers), and query it with three different natural-language questions. Compare the top_k=3 results against what your Level 1 Chroma-based CLI returned for the same queries — they should mostly agree, since both are approximating the same cosine-similarity ranking.

docs.title: 02 · Weaviate: Schemas & Hybrid Search
docs.text: Weaviate is a vector database with a schema-first design: you define collections with typed properties up front, and it can generate embeddings for you or accept your own. Its standout feature is hybrid search done natively, not bolted on.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
pip install weaviate-client

Run locally with Docker for this lesson:

docker run -d -p 8080:8080 -p 50051:50051 \
  cr.weaviate.io/semitechnologies/weaviate:1.25.0

import weaviate

client = weaviate.connect_to_local()

docs.title: Defining a collection schema
docs.text:
import weaviate.classes as wvc

client.collections.create(
    name="Article",
    properties=[
        wvc.config.Property(name="title", data_type=wvc.config.DataType.TEXT),
        wvc.config.Property(name="body", data_type=wvc.config.DataType.TEXT),
        wvc.config.Property(name="category", data_type=wvc.config.DataType.TEXT),
    ],
    vectorizer_config=wvc.config.Configure.Vectorizer.none(),
)

Unlike Chroma or Pinecone (which treat metadata as a loose dict), Weaviate wants a declared schema with types — closer to a database table than a free-form document store. This gives you type-checking on filters at query time.

docs.title: Bring-your-own-vectors vs. built-in vectorization
docs.text:
With Vectorizer.none() above, you supply vectors yourself (e.g. from sentence-transformers). Weaviate also supports built-in vectorizer modules (OpenAI, Cohere, HuggingFace) that embed text for you on insert — convenient, but it means Weaviate's server needs network access to that embedding provider. This lesson uses bring-your-own-vectors to keep things explicit and provider-agnostic.

from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer

model = SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2")
articles = client.collections.get("Article")

text = "Hybrid search blends keyword and semantic signals."
articles.data.insert(
    properties={"title": "Hybrid Search 101", "body": text, "category": "search"},
    vector=model.encode(text).tolist(),
)

docs.title: Hybrid search with alpha
docs.text:
query_vector = model.encode("how do you combine keyword and vector search").tolist()

response = articles.query.hybrid(
    query="combine keyword and vector search",
    vector=query_vector,
    alpha=0.5,
    limit=5,
)

for obj in response.objects:
    print(obj.properties["title"])

alpha is the blend weight between the two scoring methods:

  • alpha=0.0 — pure BM25 keyword search (exact term matching, classic full-text search)
  • alpha=1.0 — pure vector similarity (semantic, ignores exact wording)
  • alpha=0.5 — an even blend; a common starting point

Weaviate runs both searches, normalizes each score to [0, 1], and combines them as alpha * vector_score + (1 - alpha) * keyword_score (the actual fusion algorithm —relativeScoreFusion or rankedFusion— is configurable, but this is the mental model). The practical reason hybrid matters: pure vector search can miss an exact product code, acronym, or proper noun that a user typed verbatim, because embeddings represent meaning, not exact tokens. Keyword search catches that; vector search catches paraphrases and synonyms that keyword search misses.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Insert the same 10 documents you used in your Level 1 CLI project into a Weaviate Article collection, with real embeddings. Run the same query three times with alpha=0, alpha=0.5, and alpha=1, and compare the top-3 results at each setting. Find (or construct) one document title that contains an exact keyword your query uses but is semantically unrelated, and show how alpha shifts whether it ranks highly.

docs.title: 03 · Qdrant: Collections & Payloads
docs.text: Qdrant is an open-source vector database you can run yourself (Docker, a binary, or Kubernetes) or use as a managed cloud service. Its core unit is a "point": an ID, a vector, and a payload (arbitrary JSON metadata).

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
docker run -d -p 6333:6333 -p 6334:6334 qdrant/qdrant
pip install qdrant-client

from qdrant_client import QdrantClient

client = QdrantClient(url="http://localhost:6333")

For Qdrant Cloud instead of local Docker, swap in QdrantClient(url=..., api_key=...).

docs.title: Creating a collection
docs.text:
from qdrant_client.models import Distance, VectorParams

client.create_collection(
    collection_name="articles",
    vectors_config=VectorParams(size=384, distance=Distance.COSINE),
)

Distance also supports EUCLID and DOT — pick based on how your embedding model was trained (most sentence-transformer models are designed for cosine).

docs.title: Upserting points
docs.text:
from qdrant_client.models import PointStruct
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer

model = SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2")

docs = [
    {"id": 1, "text": "Qdrant payloads hold arbitrary metadata.", "category": "basics"},
    {"id": 2, "text": "HNSW powers Qdrant's default index.", "category": "internals"},
]

points = [
    PointStruct(
        id=doc["id"],
        vector=model.encode(doc["text"]).tolist(),
        payload={"text": doc["text"], "category": doc["category"]},
    )
    for doc in docs
]

client.upsert(collection_name="articles", points=points)

A payload is just a dict — any JSON-serializable metadata goes here: timestamps, tags, nested objects, arrays.

docs.title: Payload-filtered queries
docs.text:
from qdrant_client.models import Filter, FieldCondition, MatchValue

query_vector = model.encode("how does metadata storage work").tolist()

results = client.query_points(
    collection_name="articles",
    query=query_vector,
    query_filter=Filter(
        must=[FieldCondition(key="category", match=MatchValue(value="basics"))]
    ),
    limit=5,
)

for point in results.points:
    print(point.score, point.payload["text"])

The filter narrows the search to points matching category == "basics" before ranking by vector similarity — Qdrant pushes the filter down into the HNSW graph traversal itself (skipping non-matching nodes during the graph walk) rather than filtering a result set after the fact, which keeps recall high even with selective filters on large collections. This is a meaningfully different implementation strategy from databases that filter post-search, and it's part of why Qdrant markets itself heavily on filtered-search performance.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Create a Qdrant collection, upsert the 10 Level 1 documents with a category payload field you invent for each, and write a query that combines vector similarity with a Filter requiring a specific category. Then run the identical vector query with no filter and compare how the ranking changes — specifically note any document that would have ranked in the unfiltered top-3 but is correctly excluded by the filter.

docs.title: 04 · pgvector: Vectors Inside PostgreSQL
docs.text: pgvector is a PostgreSQL extension that adds a vector column type and distance operators. Instead of running a separate vector database, you store embeddings next to the relational data they describe — in the same table, the same transactions, the same backups.

docs.title: Installing the extension
docs.text:
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS vector;

(On managed Postgres like Supabase, Neon, or RDS, this is usually a one-click or one-command enable; self-hosted Postgres needs the pgvector package installed on the server first.)

docs.title: Creating a table with a vector column
docs.text:
CREATE TABLE articles (
    id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    title TEXT NOT NULL,
    body TEXT NOT NULL,
    embedding VECTOR(384)
);

VECTOR(384) must match your embedding model's dimension — just like Pinecone's dimension parameter, but enforced at the SQL schema level.

docs.title: Inserting embeddings
docs.text:
import psycopg2
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer

model = SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2")
conn = psycopg2.connect("dbname=mydb")
cur = conn.cursor()

text = "pgvector keeps embeddings next to relational data."
embedding = model.encode(text).tolist()

cur.execute(
    "INSERT INTO articles (title, body, embedding) VALUES (%s, %s, %s)",
    ("pgvector intro", text, embedding),
)
conn.commit()

docs.title: Nearest-neighbor queries
docs.text:
SELECT title, body, embedding <-> '[0.01, -0.02, ...]'::vector AS distance
FROM articles
ORDER BY embedding <-> '[0.01, -0.02, ...]'::vector
LIMIT 5;

pgvector gives you three distance operators:

  • <-> — Euclidean (L2) distance
  • <#> — negative inner product (for dot-product similarity)
  • <=> — cosine distance

From Python with psycopg2, pass the query vector as a parameter instead of string-formatting it:

query_vector = model.encode("how do distance operators work").tolist()

cur.execute(
    "SELECT title, body FROM articles ORDER BY embedding <=> %s::vector LIMIT 5",
    (query_vector,),
)
for row in cur.fetchall():
    print(row)

docs.title: Indexing for speed
docs.text:
Without an index, ORDER BY embedding <-> ... does a full sequential scan — fine for thousands of rows, too slow for millions. Add an HNSW index:

CREATE INDEX ON articles USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops);

Or an IVFFlat index (faster to build, slightly lower recall — covered in depth next lesson):

CREATE INDEX ON articles USING ivfflat (embedding vector_cosine_ops) WITH (lists = 100);

Note vector_cosine_ops must match the distance operator you query with (vector_l2_ops for <->, vector_ip_ops for <#>).

docs.title: When "just use Postgres" wins
docs.text: If your data already lives in Postgres and you need semantic search over, say, 10,000-5,000,000 rows with moderate query volume, pgvector lets you avoid standing up and operating an entirely separate database. You get transactional writes (insert a row and its embedding atomically with other relational updates), SQL joins between vector results and relational tables (e.g. filter by a user_id foreign key and rank by embedding distance in one query), and one less system to back up, monitor, and secure. Dedicated vector databases pull ahead at very large scale (hundreds of millions+ of vectors) or when you need features pgvector doesn't offer, like Pinecone/Weaviate-style namespacing or built-in hybrid fusion scoring.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Set up a local Postgres with pgvector (Docker image pgvector/pgvector:pg16 is the fastest path), create the articles table above, insert your 10 Level 1 documents with real embeddings, and write one SQL query that both filters by a WHERE title ILIKE '%keyword%' condition and orders by <=> cosine distance — something no pure vector database in this level can do in a single native query without a client-side join.

docs.title: 05 · How HNSW Actually Works
docs.text: Every database you've used so far (Chroma, Pinecone, Qdrant, pgvector's HNSW index) defaults to the same algorithm under the hood: Hierarchical Navigable Small World graphs. Level 1 introduced the idea conceptually. This lesson goes inside it.

docs.title: The problem HNSW solves
docs.text: Brute-force search (Level 1, lesson 4) compares your query against every vector: O(n). A flat navigable small-world graph — a single layer where each vector links to its nearest neighbors — turns search into a greedy graph walk, which is much faster on average, but can still take many hops to cross a large, spread-out graph, and can get stuck in a locally-good-but-globally-wrong region. HNSW fixes both by stacking multiple layers of that graph on top of each other.

docs.title: Building the layers
docs.text:
Each vector is inserted into layer 0 (the bottom layer, containing all vectors) and, with exponentially decreasing probability, into higher layers too. A rough mental model with branching factor-like decay:

Layer 2:        •                       •              (very few nodes)
Layer 1:        •        •      •       •      •       (some nodes)
Layer 0:  • • •  • •  • • • •  •  • • •  • • • •  • •   (every node)

Layer 0 has every vector and dense, short-range links. Each layer up has exponentially fewer vectors and longer-range links. The top layer might have only a handful of nodes — just enough to act as highway on-ramps into the rest of the graph.

docs.title: Searching: greedy descent through layers
docs.text:
1. Start at a fixed entry point in the top layer.
  2. Greedy search within the current layer: repeatedly move to whichever neighbor is closer to the query than your current position, until no neighbor improves (a local minimum for this layer).
  3. Drop down one layer, using the local minimum you just found as the new starting point.
  4. Repeat the greedy search at the new layer. Because the previous layer narrowed you down to roughly the right neighborhood, this layer's greedy search only needs a few more hops to refine further.
  5. Continue until you've done a final greedy search at layer 0, maintaining a candidate list of the ef_search best vectors seen, and return the top k.

This is why the top layer can be sparse and still useful: it's not trying to be accurate, it's trying to get you to roughly the right region of the graph in a handful of long jumps, so that lower layers only need short jumps to refine.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
• M (max connections per node): how many neighbor links each node keeps per layer. Higher M means denser graphs, better recall, more memory, slower inserts. Typical values: 12-48.
  • ef_construction: how large a candidate list is explored while building the graph (choosing which neighbors to link). Higher values build a higher-quality graph at the cost of slower index construction.
  • ef_search: how large a candidate list is explored while querying. Higher values improve recall (closer to true nearest neighbors) at the cost of slower queries. This is the main knob you tune at query time without rebuilding the index — most databases expose it directly (Qdrant's hnsw_ef, pgvector's hnsw.ef_search session setting).
  • Why it's "approximate": greedy search can still terminate at a local minimum that isn't the true global nearest neighbor, especially with ef values set low. Recall (the fraction of true top-k results actually returned) typically lands in the 95-99.9% range for reasonable settings — good enough for nearly every real application, and the gap closes as ef increases.
  • Insertion cost: every insert runs a search (to find where to link the new node) plus graph updates at multiple layers, which is why HNSW indexes are noticeably slower to build than to query, and why very write-heavy workloads sometimes prefer IVF-based indexes (next lesson) or batch rebuilding.
  • Memory: the full graph — all nodes' neighbor lists across all layers — typically lives in RAM for query speed, which is why HNSW memory usage scales with M and vector count, and is often the dominant cost driver for self-hosted vector databases at scale.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: In Qdrant (lesson 3) or pgvector (lesson 4), create two collections/indexes over the same 10,000+ vector dataset (synthetic random vectors are fine for this) — one with a low ef_search/M and one with a high value — and measure both query latency and recall@10 (compare each approximate result set against a brute-force ground truth computed with NumPy, as in Level 1 lesson 4). Report the latency/recall tradeoff you observe.

docs.title: 06 · IVF & Product Quantization
docs.text: HNSW (previous lesson) trades memory for speed: the whole graph lives in RAM. At billion-vector scale, that memory bill gets enormous. IVF (Inverted File Index) and Product Quantization (PQ) are a different pair of tricks — often used together — that trade a little accuracy for dramatically less memory and, for IVF, fewer distance computations per query.

docs.title: Inverted File Index (IVF): cluster first, search locally
docs.text:
1. Build time: run k-means clustering on a sample of your vectors to produce nlist cluster centroids (e.g. nlist=1024). Every vector in the dataset is then assigned to its nearest centroid — this is its "inverted list."
  2. Query time: compare the query vector against only the nlist centroids (cheap — there are far fewer centroids than vectors), find the nprobe closest centroids, and only search the vectors inside those lists.
import faiss
import numpy as np

d = 384
nlist = 1024
quantizer = faiss.IndexFlatL2(d)
index = faiss.IndexIVFFlat(quantizer, d, nlist)

vectors = np.random.random((100_000, d)).astype("float32")
index.train(vectors)   # runs k-means to find centroids
index.add(vectors)

index.nprobe = 16       # search the 16 nearest clusters out of 1024
distances, ids = index.search(np.random.random((1, d)).astype("float32"), k=5)

If a dataset has 10 million vectors spread across 1024 clusters (~10,000 vectors each) and you set nprobe=16, you're scanning roughly 160,000 vectors instead of 10 million — a ~60x reduction, at the cost of possibly missing a true neighbor that happened to land in a nearby-but-unsearched cluster (this is IVF's source of approximation, distinct from HNSW's).

docs.title: Product Quantization (PQ): compress the vectors themselves
docs.text:
IVF reduces how many vectors you compare against. PQ reduces how expensive each comparison is, by compressing each vector.

  1. Split each d-dimensional vector into m equal-length subvectors (e.g. a 384-dim vector split into m=8 subvectors of 48 dimensions each).
  2. For each of the m subvector positions, run k-means independently to learn a small codebook of (commonly) 256 centroids.
  3. Store each original vector as just m codebook indices (e.g. 8 bytes total — one byte per subvector, since 256 centroids fit in a uint8) instead of d floats (384 × 4 bytes = 1536 bytes).
m = 8          # number of subvector chunks
nbits = 8      # bits per code → 2^8 = 256 centroids per chunk
pq_index = faiss.IndexIVFPQ(quantizer, d, nlist, m, nbits)
pq_index.train(vectors)
pq_index.add(vectors)

Distance between a query and a compressed vector is computed approximately using precomputed lookup tables between the query's subvectors and each chunk's codebook — not by decompressing back to full floats, which is what makes PQ fast and memory-cheap simultaneously, not just memory-cheap.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
• Why cluster first (IVF): a flat/brute-force scan is O(n) per query. IVF turns that into O(nlist) (compare against centroids) + O(n/nlist * nprobe) (scan only the probed lists) — a large win when nlist is well-chosen relative to n.
  • The nprobe tradeoff: nprobe=1 only searches the single nearest cluster — fast but misses any true neighbor whose cluster boundary happened to separate it from the query. Increasing nprobe toward nlist approaches brute-force accuracy at brute-force cost; there's no free lunch, only a slider. "Boundary problem": a query near a cluster edge may have its true nearest neighbor sitting just across that edge in an unsearched cluster — this is IVF's main failure mode, and why nprobe > 1 is almost always used in practice. "Boundary problem" is why real deployments rarely use nprobe=1.
  • Why PQ compression doesn't ruin accuracy outright: subvector codebooks are trained on real data distribution (via k-means), so the quantization error per chunk is small relative to the chunk's own variance — not uniform random noise. Still, PQ alone (without IVF) is a lossy approximation of distance, so recall drops somewhat versus exact float comparison; this is the accuracy half of the tradeoff, paid for 16-32x memory reduction.
  • IVF+PQ together: the combination (IndexIVFPQ above) is the classic "fits in RAM at billion-scale" recipe — IVF narrows the candidate set, PQ makes each candidate comparison and each vector's storage footprint tiny. This is roughly what Pinecone, Milvus, and FAISS-backed systems use under the hood at very large scale, often layered with additional re-ranking against exact vectors for the final top candidates to recover some of PQ's lost precision.
  • HNSW vs. IVF+PQ, operationally: HNSW generally wins on recall and query latency when memory isn't the binding constraint. IVF+PQ wins when the dataset is too large to fit as a full-precision graph in available RAM — the classic scale-vs-accuracy fork in the road (this sets up next lesson's decision framework).

Measure index memory footprint (faiss indexes can be written to disk with faiss.write_index — compare file sizes), query latency for 100 queries, and recall@10 against a brute-force IndexFlatL2 ground truth. Report which index you'd pick for a 10-million-vector dataset with a 2GB RAM budget, and why.

docs.title: 07 · Choosing the Right Index
docs.text: You now know four production databases and the two dominant index families behind them. This lesson is the decision framework for picking between them on a real project.

docs.title: The index decision tree
docs.text:
Dataset fits comfortably in RAM as a full HNSW graph?
  ├─ Yes → use HNSW (best recall/latency for the memory you're already paying for)
  └─ No, RAM-constrained or huge scale (100M+ vectors)
        → use IVF+PQ (trade some recall for ~16-32x memory reduction)

Write-heavy workload (constant inserts/updates, low tolerance for rebuild lag)?
  → lean toward IVF (cheaper incremental inserts into existing clusters)
     or a managed service that hides rebalancing from you (Pinecone)

Need exact results, not approximate (small dataset, correctness-critical)?
  → brute-force / flat index is fine under ~100K-1M vectors on modern hardware

Recall requirement matters more than most people assume up front: a recommendation system tolerating occasional "good enough" neighbors can run ef_search/nprobe low and go faster; a legal or medical retrieval system that needs the actual nearest match for every query should bias toward higher ef/nprobe or brute-force, accepting the latency cost.

docs.title: Comparing the four databases from this level
docs.text: Pinecone Weaviate Qdrant pgvector Hosting Managed only (serverless) Managed or self-hosted Managed or self-hosted Self-hosted (any Postgres) or managed Postgres Default index Proprietary (HNSW-like, hidden) HNSW HNSW HNSW or IVFFlat (your choice) Native hybrid search Sparse-dense hybrid support Yes, alpha-tunable Yes (via sparse vectors) No (would need separate full-text search + join) Payload/metadata filtering Yes Yes Yes, with graph-level filter push-down Yes, via ordinary SQL WHERE Pricing model Per read/write unit + storage Self-host: infra cost; managed: usage-based Self-host: infra cost; managed: usage-based Whatever you already pay for Postgres Best fit Teams that want zero ops Teams wanting schema + hybrid search built in Teams wanting self-hosted control + strong filtering Teams whose data is already relational and don't want a second database

docs.title: A practical heuristic
docs.text:
For most new projects, start with the simplest option that meets your recall and latency needs, and only move to something more specialized when you hit a real limit:

  1. Under ~1M vectors, already using Postgres → pgvector. No new infrastructure, transactional consistency with your other data.
  2. Need managed, zero-ops, scaling to tens of millions → Pinecone.
  3. Need self-hosted control, heavy payload filtering, or on-prem requirements → Qdrant.
  4. Need schema validation and native hybrid search out of the box → Weaviate.
  5. Hundreds of millions+ vectors, RAM-constrained → look beyond this level's four options toward IVF+PQ-first systems (Milvus, FAISS-backed custom services) — the previous lesson's tradeoff becomes unavoidable at this scale.

None of these choices are permanent or mutually exclusive — many real systems use pgvector for a transactional "source of truth" table and periodically sync a subset into a dedicated vector database for high-QPS semantic search, getting both consistency and scale.

docs.title: 08 · Batch Upserts & Data Pipelines
docs.text: Every lesson so far has upserted one or two vectors at a time for clarity. Real pipelines embed and write thousands to millions of vectors, and doing that one-at-a-time is slow and fragile. This lesson covers batching, idempotency, and a reusable ETL shape.

docs.title: Why batching matters
docs.text:
A single upsert call has fixed per-request overhead (network round-trip, server- side bookkeeping) on top of the actual write. Batch requests amortize that overhead across many vectors:

# Slow: one network round-trip per vector
for doc in docs:
    index.upsert(vectors=[build_vector(doc)])

# Fast: one round-trip per batch
BATCH_SIZE = 100
for i in range(0, len(docs), BATCH_SIZE):
    batch = docs[i:i + BATCH_SIZE]
    index.upsert(vectors=[build_vector(d) for d in batch])

Most databases document a recommended batch size (Pinecone suggests keeping batches under ~2MB of payload; Qdrant and Weaviate have similar guidance) — check before assuming bigger is always better, since oversized batches can hit request size limits or timeout.

docs.title: Idempotent upserts via deterministic IDs
docs.text:
If you re-run an embedding pipeline (say, after fixing a bug in your chunking logic), you want it to overwrite the old vectors for the same source content, not create duplicates alongside them. The fix is to derive each vector's ID deterministically from its source, instead of using an auto-incrementing counter or a random UUID:

import hashlib

def deterministic_id(source_path: str, chunk_index: int) -> str:
    raw = f"{source_path}::{chunk_index}"
    return hashlib.sha256(raw.encode()).hexdigest()[:24]

Running the pipeline twice over the same file now produces the same IDs both times, so the second run's upserts cleanly replace the first run's vectors instead of piling up duplicates. This matters enormously in practice — it's the difference between a pipeline you can safely re-run and one you have to carefully track state for externally.

docs.title: A simple ETL pipeline pattern
docs.text:
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer

model = SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2")

def chunk_text(text: str, chunk_size: int = 500, overlap: int = 50) -> list[str]:
    chunks = []
    start = 0
    while start < len(text):
        chunks.append(text[start:start + chunk_size])
        start += chunk_size - overlap
    return chunks

def process_source(source_path: str, source_text: str) -> list[dict]:
    chunks = chunk_text(source_text)
    embeddings = model.encode(chunks)  # batch-encodes all chunks at once
    return [
        {
            "id": deterministic_id(source_path, i),
            "values": embeddings[i].tolist(),
            "metadata": {"source": source_path, "chunk_index": i, "text": chunks[i]},
        }
        for i in range(len(chunks))
    ]

def run_pipeline(sources: dict[str, str], index, batch_size: int = 100):
    all_vectors = []
    for path, text in sources.items():
        all_vectors.extend(process_source(path, text))

    for i in range(0, len(all_vectors), batch_size):
        batch = all_vectors[i:i + batch_size]
        index.upsert(vectors=batch)

Note model.encode(chunks) is called once per source on the whole list of chunks, not once per chunk — sentence-transformers batches encoding internally and is dramatically faster that way than calling .encode() in a loop.

docs.title: Handling partial batch failures
docs.text:
A batch of 100 can fail entirely (network error, rate limit) or partially (some databases report per-item errors within a batch response). A simple and robust retry strategy:

import time

def upsert_with_retry(index, vectors: list[dict], max_retries: int = 3):
    for attempt in range(max_retries):
        try:
            index.upsert(vectors=vectors)
            return
        except Exception as e:
            if attempt == max_retries - 1:
                raise
            time.sleep(2 ** attempt)  # exponential backoff: 1s, 2s, 4s

Because upserts are idempotent (same deterministic ID → same result), retrying a whole failed batch is always safe — you'll never end up with duplicates from a retry, only from a genuinely new ID.
