docs.text: Extend the pipeline above to process a folder of .txt files (reuse your Level 1 project's input folder), write it to the vector database of your choice from this level, then run the exact same pipeline a second time with no changes to the input files and confirm via the database's item count (e.g. Qdrant's collection info, or index.describe_index_stats() in Pinecone) that no duplicate vectors were created.

docs.title: 09 · Namespaces, Sharding & Multi-Tenancy
docs.text: Building a product used by many customers (a SaaS app, not a single internal tool) raises a question none of the previous lessons addressed: how do you keep Customer A's vectors from ever appearing in Customer B's search results — and do it without provisioning a separate database per customer?

docs.title: Namespaces: logical isolation within one index
docs.text:
Pinecone's answer is namespaces — a partition key built into the upsert and query calls:

# Each tenant's vectors live in their own namespace
index.upsert(vectors=tenant_a_vectors, namespace="tenant-a")
index.upsert(vectors=tenant_b_vectors, namespace="tenant-b")

# A query against one namespace never sees another namespace's vectors
results = index.query(vector=query_vector, top_k=5, namespace="tenant-a")

Crucially, a query scoped to namespace="tenant-a" has the same latency whether there are 10 namespaces or 10,000 sharing the index — the namespace boundary is enforced at the index level, not implemented as a metadata filter applied after search. This matters for predictable multi-tenant performance.

Qdrant and Weaviate don't have a dedicated "namespace" primitive with that exact name, but achieve the same isolation two ways:

  • Metadata/payload filtering: tag every point with tenant_id and always filter by it (Qdrant's filtered search pushes this into the HNSW traversal itself — see lesson 3 — so it stays reasonably fast, but it's not a hard architectural boundary the way a namespace is).
  • One collection per tenant: Qdrant and Weaviate collections are cheap enough to create many of, so some teams give each tenant (or tenant tier) its own collection instead — this is architecturally closer to Pinecone namespaces.

docs.title: Sharding for scale
docs.text:
Sharding splits a dataset across multiple machines when it's too large (or too high-throughput) for one node. Two common strategies:

  1. Hash-based sharding: route each vector to a shard based on a hash of its ID. Simple, spreads load evenly, but a query normally has to fan out to every shard (since any shard could hold the nearest neighbor) and merge results — more network overhead per query.
  2. Tenant-based sharding: route all of one tenant's vectors to the same shard (e.g. shard = hash(tenant_id) % num_shards). Queries for a given tenant only hit one shard — much cheaper per query — but shard sizes can grow unevenly if tenants vary wildly in size (a "hot shard" problem), and a single huge tenant can still outgrow one shard.

Managed services (Pinecone, Weaviate Cloud, Qdrant Cloud) handle sharding internally and mostly invisibly; self-hosting at real scale means choosing and operating one of these strategies yourself.

docs.title: One-index-per-tenant vs. shared-index-with-filter
docs.text:
One index per tenant Shared index + namespace/filter Isolation Strongest (physically separate) Strong (logically separate) Cost at scale with many small tenants High (per-index overhead × tenant count) Low (overhead amortized) Noisy-neighbor risk None (fully isolated) Low with true namespaces, higher with filter-only isolation Operational complexity High (manage N indexes) Low (manage 1 index) Good fit Few large tenants, strict isolation requirements (e.g. regulated data) Many small-to-medium tenants, cost-sensitive

A common pattern: shared index with namespaces for most tenants, with an escape hatch to a dedicated index for a handful of enterprise customers who require stronger isolation guarantees or have outgrown what a shared index can serve efficiently.

docs.title: 10 · Project — Multi-Source RAG Retrieval Service
docs.text: This level's capstone: build a small web service that ingests documents from two different source types, stores them with source-tracking metadata, and exposes a search endpoint that queries across both — the retrieval half of a real RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) system.

docs.title: What you're building
docs.text:
A FastAPI service with two responsibilities:

  1. Ingestion: pull content from (a) local .txt files and (b) a web page's text content, chunk and embed both, and upsert them into one Qdrant collection (or a pgvector table) with a source_type field ("file" or "web") and a source_ref field (file path or URL).

  "results": [
    {
      "text": "Batch requests amortize per-request overhead across many vectors...",
      "source_type": "file",

docs.title: Why dense search alone isn't enough
docs.text:
Dense embeddings are great at matching meaning. Ask for "how do I reset my password" and a dense retriever will happily surface a document that says "recovering account access" — no shared words, same intent.

But dense retrieval is surprisingly bad at exact matches: product SKUs, error codes, rare proper nouns, part numbers, acronyms. A query like ERR_CONN_RESET or SKU-48213-B often gets embedded into a vague "this looks like an error code" region of space, and the one document that contains that exact string can lose to five documents that are merely topically similar.

Classic keyword search (BM25) is the mirror image: perfect on exact terms, useless on paraphrase. Hybrid search runs both and merges the results.

docs.title: BM25 in five lines
docs.text:
Install rank_bm25:

pip install rank_bm25

from rank_bm25 import BM25Okapi

corpus = [
    "Connection reset error ERR_CONN_RESET occurs when the TLS handshake times out",
    "To recover your account, reset your password from the login screen",
    "SKU-48213-B is the replacement part for the model X200 fan assembly",
    "Semantic search uses dense vector embeddings to rank documents by meaning",
]

tokenized_corpus = [doc.lower().split() for doc in corpus]
bm25 = BM25Okapi(tokenized_corpus)

query = "ERR_CONN_RESET"
scores = bm25.get_scores(query.lower().split())
print(scores)
# doc 0 (the exact error code) scores far above the rest

BM25 scores each document by term frequency (how often query terms appear) weighted by inverse document frequency (how rare those terms are across the whole corpus) and normalized for document length. It has no notion of meaning — ERR_CONN_RESET and connection reset are different tokens to it — but it is unbeatable when the query contains the literal string you need.

docs.title: Running dense and sparse side by side
docs.text:
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
import numpy as np

model = SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2")
doc_embeddings = model.encode(corpus, normalize_embeddings=True)

def dense_search(query, top_k=4):
    q_emb = model.encode([query], normalize_embeddings=True)[0]
    sims = doc_embeddings @ q_emb
    ranked = np.argsort(-sims)
    return [(int(i), float(sims[i])) for i in ranked[:top_k]]

def sparse_search(query, top_k=4):
    scores = bm25.get_scores(query.lower().split())
    ranked = np.argsort(-scores)
    return [(int(i), float(scores[i])) for i in ranked[:top_k]]

query = "how do I recover my login"
print("dense :", dense_search(query))
print("sparse:", sparse_search(query))

For a paraphrased query like this, dense search ranks doc 1 (the password reset doc) highly even though it shares almost no words with the query. Sparse search, with no overlapping tokens beyond "my", ranks it poorly. That asymmetry is exactly why you want both running at once.

docs.title: Combining results with Reciprocal Rank Fusion
docs.text:
You now have two ranked lists with incompatible scales — BM25 scores are unbounded term-frequency weights, cosine similarity is bounded in [-1, 1]. You can't just add them. Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) sidesteps the scale problem entirely by fusing on rank position, not raw score.

def rrf_fuse(rankings: list[list[int]], k: int = 60) -> list[tuple[int, float]]:
    """rankings: list of ranked doc-id lists (best first), one per retriever."""
    scores: dict[int, float] = {}
    for ranking in rankings:
        for rank, doc_id in enumerate(ranking):
            scores[doc_id] = scores.get(doc_id, 0.0) + 1.0 / (k + rank + 1)
    return sorted(scores.items(), key=lambda pair: -pair[1])

dense_ids = [doc_id for doc_id, _ in dense_search(query, top_k=4)]
sparse_ids = [doc_id for doc_id, _ in sparse_search(query, top_k=4)]

fused = rrf_fuse([dense_ids, sparse_ids])
print(fused)

A document that ranks well in either list gets a meaningful score boost; a document that ranks well in both rises to the top. No tuning of relative weights required — that's the whole appeal of RRF over naive score averaging.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
1. Why rank, not score. Different retrievers produce scores on incomparable scales (and sometimes non-linear ones — BM25 scores for a 2-word query and a 10-word query aren't directly comparable either). Rank position is always comparable: "1st place" means the same thing regardless of retriever.
  2. The formula. For each retriever r and each document d, RRF contributes 1 / (k + rank_r(d) + 1). These contributions are summed across retrievers. A document absent from a retriever's list simply contributes 0 from that retriever.
  3. The constant k. k (commonly 60) dampens the difference between adjacent ranks. Without it, rank 1 vs. rank 2 would differ by 50% (1/1 vs 1/2); with k=60, it's under 2% (1/61 vs 1/62). Larger k makes fusion more forgiving of a retriever getting the exact top spot wrong by one or two positions.
  4. Why it beats weighted score averaging in practice. Picking weights for score averaging (e.g. 0.7 * dense + 0.3 * sparse) requires tuning per-dataset and breaks when one retriever's score distribution shifts. RRF needs no such tuning and is remarkably robust across very different retrieval signals — it's the default fusion method in most production hybrid-search stacks (Elasticsearch, Vespa, Weaviate's hybrid mode).
  5. What it doesn't fix. RRF assumes each retriever's ranking is individually decent. If one retriever's list is essentially random, RRF will still let its noise dilute the final ranking somewhat — it's a merging strategy, not a quality filter. That's what re-ranking (next lesson) is for.

Write a hybrid_search(query, top_k) function that runs dense_search and sparse_search over the full corpus, fuses with rrf_fuse, and returns the top-k fused results. Try three queries — one that's pure keyword, one that's pure paraphrase, one that's a mix — and confirm hybrid search beats both individual retrievers on the mixed query.

docs.title: The two-stage pattern
docs.text:
Every retriever you've used so far — Chroma, Pinecone, Qdrant, pgvector — is a bi-encoder: the query and each document are embedded independently, then compared with cosine similarity or dot product. That's what makes them fast — document embeddings are precomputed once, and a query only needs one new embedding plus a nearest-neighbor lookup.

But independence has a cost: the model never sees the query and a specific document together. It can't notice "this document mentions the right topic but answers the opposite question" — it only sees two points in space and a distance between them.

The fix used in nearly every production RAG and search system is a two-stage pipeline:

  1. Retrieve a wide net of candidates (say, top 50) cheaply with your existing bi-encoder vector search.
  2. Re-rank those 50 with a slower, much more accurate cross-encoder that looks at the query and each document jointly, then keep only the top 5-10 for your LLM or user.

docs.title: Re-ranking with a cross-encoder
docs.text:
pip install sentence-transformers

from sentence_transformers import CrossEncoder

reranker = CrossEncoder("cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2")

query = "What causes a connection reset error during a TLS handshake?"

candidates = [
    "Connection reset error ERR_CONN_RESET occurs when the TLS handshake times out before both sides agree on a cipher suite.",
    "To recover your account, reset your password from the login screen using the forgot-password link.",
    "SKU-48213-B is the replacement part for the model X200 fan assembly.",
    "TLS handshakes can fail due to clock skew, mismatched cipher suites, or an expired certificate.",
]

pairs = [[query, doc] for doc in candidates]
scores = reranker.predict(pairs)

ranked = sorted(zip(candidates, scores), key=lambda pair: -pair[1])
for doc, score in ranked:
    print(f"{score:.3f}  {doc[:70]}")

The two TLS-related documents (0 and 3) score far above the password-reset and SKU documents — and crucially, the model can distinguish between "causes a connection reset" (doc 0) and "handshake failures in general" (doc 3) in a way plain embedding similarity often can't, because it reads them side by side with the query rather than comparing two independently-computed points.

docs.title: Wiring it into a retrieval pipeline
docs.text:
def search_and_rerank(query, collection, retrieve_k=50, final_k=5):
    # Stage 1: cheap, wide retrieval from your vector DB
    results = collection.query(query_texts=[query], n_results=retrieve_k)
    candidates = results["documents"][0]

    # Stage 2: precise, narrow re-ranking
    pairs = [[query, doc] for doc in candidates]
    scores = reranker.predict(pairs)

    ranked = sorted(zip(candidates, scores), key=lambda pair: -pair[1])
    return ranked[:final_k]

Note the shape: retrieve wide, rank narrow. If you retrieve only 5 candidates from the vector DB and re-rank those 5, you've only reordered — you gain nothing if the actually best document wasn't in the top 5 to begin with. Retrieving 50-100 candidates before re-ranking is what gives the cross-encoder room to rescue a document the bi-encoder under-ranked.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
1. Bi-encoder architecture. Two independent forward passes: embed(query) and embed(document), each producing a fixed-size vector with no knowledge of the other input. Similarity is a cheap vector operation computed after both embeddings exist — this is why they can be precomputed and indexed for millions of documents.
  2. Cross-encoder architecture. One forward pass: the query and document are concatenated (typically [CLS] query [SEP] document [SEP]) and fed through the transformer together. Every token of the query can attend to every token of the document, and vice versa, at every layer. The model outputs a single relevance score directly — there's no embedding to compare, no vector space at all.
  3. Why this makes cross-encoders slower. Because the document representation depends on the specific query, nothing can be precomputed. Scoring N documents against a query means N full forward passes through the transformer, every single time. That's why cross-encoders re-rank tens of candidates, not millions.
  4. Why this makes cross-encoders more accurate. Joint attention lets the model pick up on negation, specificity, and relational cues ("causes X" vs. "related to X in general") that two independently-pooled embeddings simply discard. In practice, cross-encoders consistently beat bi-encoders on reranking benchmarks like MS MARCO by a wide margin.
  5. The practical rule of thumb. Retrieve ~10-20x more candidates than you actually need with the fast bi-encoder, then let the cross-encoder cut that down to your final result count. This gets you most of the accuracy of "score everything with a cross-encoder" at a tiny fraction of the latency cost.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Build on your Chroma collection from Level 1/2. Write search_and_rerank as shown, retrieving retrieve_k=30 candidates and re-ranking to final_k=5. Pick a query where you suspect the bi-encoder's raw top-5 and the re-ranked top-5 will differ, print both lists side by side, and note which documents moved and why that makes sense given what a cross-encoder can see that a bi-encoder can't.

docs.title: Why chunking matters as much as the model
docs.text:
A 50-page PDF can't be embedded as one vector and usefully searched — the embedding would be an average of everything in the document, diluting any specific fact a query might be looking for. So every real system splits documents into chunks before embedding. How you split has a bigger effect on retrieval quality than which embedding model you pick.

Two failure modes to keep in mind:

  • Chunks too small — a sentence fragment without its surrounding context ("...which fixes the issue.") is technically retrievable but useless once retrieved, and the LLM reading it has no idea what "the issue" was.
  • Chunks too large — the one relevant sentence gets averaged in with nine irrelevant ones, so the chunk's embedding doesn't actually land near queries about that one sentence anymore.

docs.title: Fixed-size chunking
docs.text:
The simplest approach: split by character or token count, with overlap so you don't sever a sentence exactly at a chunk boundary.

def fixed_size_chunks(text: str, chunk_size: int = 500, overlap: int = 50):
    chunks = []
    start = 0
    while start < len(text):
        end = start + chunk_size
        chunks.append(text[start:end])
        start = end - overlap  # step back so chunks overlap
    return chunks

Overlap (commonly 10-20% of chunk size) means a fact split across two chunks by bad luck still appears whole in at least one of them. The downside: fixed boundaries ignore sentence and paragraph structure entirely — a chunk can start mid-sentence.

docs.title: Sentence- and paragraph-aware chunking
docs.text:
Better: split on structure first, then pack sentences/paragraphs into chunks up to a target size.

import re

def sentence_aware_chunks(text: str, max_chars: int = 500):
    sentences = re.split(r"(?<=[.!?])\s+", text.strip())
    chunks, current = [], ""
    for sentence in sentences:
        if len(current) + len(sentence) > max_chars and current:
            chunks.append(current.strip())
            current = ""
        current += sentence + " "
    if current.strip():
        chunks.append(current.strip())
    return chunks

This never cuts a sentence in half. In practice, most production systems chunk at the paragraph level first (splitting on blank lines or markdown headers) and only fall back to sentence-level splitting for paragraphs that exceed the max size on their own.

docs.title: Semantic chunking
docs.text:
The most content-aware approach: embed each sentence, then split wherever the similarity between adjacent sentences drops sharply — the idea being that a topic shift in the text shows up as a drop in embedding similarity between consecutive sentences.

import numpy as np
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer

model = SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2")

def semantic_chunks(text: str, drop_threshold: float = 0.3):
    sentences = re.split(r"(?<=[.!?])\s+", text.strip())
    if len(sentences) < 2:
        return [text]

    embeddings = model.encode(sentences, normalize_embeddings=True)
    sims = [float(embeddings[i] @ embeddings[i + 1]) for i in range(len(embeddings) - 1)]

    chunks, current = [], [sentences[0]]
    for i, sim in enumerate(sims):
        if sim < drop_threshold:
            chunks.append(" ".join(current))
            current = []
        current.append(sentences[i + 1])
    chunks.append(" ".join(current))
    return chunks

This is noticeably slower (every sentence needs an embedding) and the threshold needs tuning per-domain, but it tends to produce chunks that align with actual topic boundaries rather than an arbitrary character count — useful for long-form documents like reports or transcripts where a fixed size would frequently split a self-contained idea in two.

docs.title: Choosing chunk size for your retriever
docs.text:
A rough starting point, assuming you embed with a model like all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (256-token context) or a larger model (512+ tokens):

Chunk size Good for Risk 100-200 tokens FAQ-style, precise fact lookup loses surrounding context 300-500 tokens general-purpose RAG the sweet spot for most document types 800+ tokens summarization-style retrieval embedding dilutes specific facts

Always test empirically (lesson 5 covers how) — the "right" chunk size is whatever maximizes recall@k on your own eval set, not a number from a blog post.

docs.text: Take a multi-paragraph document (a few pages of prose — a README, an article). Chunk it three ways: fixed-size (500 chars, 50 overlap), sentence-aware (500 chars), and semantic. For each chunking strategy, embed the chunks and run the same 3 queries against each resulting chunk set. Compare: which strategy puts the actually-relevant chunk in the top result most consistently? Note any case where a fixed-size chunk split a fact in half and hurt a query's result.

docs.title: How to pick an embedding model
docs.text:
Every embedding model trades off along the same four axes:

  • Quality — how well it ranks relevant-vs-irrelevant documents on benchmark tasks. The MTEB leaderboard (Massive Text Embedding Benchmark) is the standard reference: it scores hundreds of models across retrieval, classification, and clustering tasks.
  • Dimensionality — all-MiniLM-L6-v2 produces 384-dim vectors; text-embedding-3-large can produce up to 3072. Higher dimensionality usually means better quality but more storage and slower search.
  • Max sequence length — how much text one embedding call can see before truncating. A model with a 256-token limit silently drops the rest of a long chunk; a 512+ token model handles longer chunks without truncation.
  • Latency and cost — a small local model like all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (22M parameters) embeds thousands of documents per second on a CPU and costs nothing per call. A hosted API model may rank higher on MTEB but adds network latency and a per-token bill at scale.
# Comparing two models on the same small eval set
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
import numpy as np

small_model = SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2")       # 384-dim, fast, free
big_model = SentenceTransformer("all-mpnet-base-v2")         # 768-dim, slower, higher quality

queries = ["how does TLS handshake failure happen"]
docs = [
    "TLS handshakes fail due to cipher mismatch or expired certificates",
    "Our return policy allows 30 days for unopened items",
]

for name, model in [("MiniLM", small_model), ("MPNet", big_model)]:
    q = model.encode(queries, normalize_embeddings=True)[0]
    d = model.encode(docs, normalize_embeddings=True)
    sims = d @ q
    print(name, sims)

For most RAG applications, start with a small, fast, open model (all-MiniLM-L6-v2 or similar) and only move to something larger/hosted if your eval set (lesson 5) actually shows it's not good enough — "biggest model on MTEB" is rarely the right default, since the gap often doesn't matter for your specific domain and the latency/cost difference is real.

docs.title: When fine-tuning is worth it
docs.text:
A general-purpose embedding model is trained on broad web text. If your domain uses specialized vocabulary — internal product names, legal/medical jargon, a company's own acronyms — the general model may genuinely not know which documents are "close" in your domain's sense, no matter how well it scores on MTEB. That's the signal to fine-tune: your own eval set shows plateauing recall that re-ranking and better chunking don't fix.

Fine-tuning here means further training a model on your own (query, relevant_document) pairs so it learns your domain's notion of relevance, without needing labeled negative examples.

pip install sentence-transformers

from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer, InputExample, losses
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader

model = SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2")

# Your own labeled pairs: queries matched to their one correct document
train_examples = [
    InputExample(texts=["how do I reset ERR_CONN_RESET", "ERR_CONN_RESET occurs when the TLS handshake times out"]),
    InputExample(texts=["password recovery steps", "reset your password from the login screen"]),
    # ... hundreds to thousands of real pairs from your own query logs or support tickets
]

train_dataloader = DataLoader(train_examples, shuffle=True, batch_size=16)
train_loss = losses.MultipleNegativesRankingLoss(model)

model.fit(
    train_objectives=[(train_dataloader, train_loss)],
    epochs=3,
    warmup_steps=100,
    output_path="./fine-tuned-domain-model",
)

Where do the pairs come from in practice? Query logs paired with the document the user actually clicked or found useful, support tickets paired with their resolving KB article, or — if you have none of that yet — an LLM can bootstrap synthetic (query, document) pairs from your corpus to get started before you have real usage data.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
1. In-batch negatives. MultipleNegativesRankingLoss needs only positive pairs — it builds negatives automatically from the rest of the batch. For a batch of 16 (query, document) pairs, each query's own document is the positive, and the other 15 documents in the batch become its negatives for that training step.
  2. The contrastive objective. The loss pushes each query's embedding closer to its true document's embedding (higher cosine similarity) and simultaneously pushes it away from the 15 in-batch negatives (lower similarity). Over many batches and epochs, this reshapes the embedding space so your domain's query-document pairs cluster together.
  3. Why larger batches help. More in-batch negatives per step means a harder, more informative training signal — the model has to distinguish the true match from more competitors at once. This is why fine-tuning recipes often push batch size as high as GPU memory allows.
  4. What actually changes in the model. Fine-tuning doesn't memorize your documents or "store" answers anywhere — it adjusts the transformer's weights so that the function mapping text to a vector places your domain's related pairs nearer each other than the pretrained weights did. The model still generalizes to unseen text; it's just been nudged toward your domain's geometry.
  5. The failure mode to watch for. With too few training pairs or too many epochs, the model overfits to your training pairs specifically and loses some of its general-purpose quality on anything outside that distribution. Always re-run your eval set (next lesson) after fine-tuning, including on queries not in the training set, before deciding to deploy it.

docs.title: Two different questions
docs.text:
"Is my vector search good?" is actually two separate questions that need separate measurements:

  1. Quality — does it return the right documents? (recall@k)
  2. Speed — how fast does it return them, especially under load? (latency percentiles)

Tuning one often costs you the other — that's the whole reason to measure both before touching any settings.

docs.title: Measuring recall@k against ground truth
docs.text:
You need a small labeled eval set: a list of (query, relevant_doc_ids) pairs where you (or domain experts) have manually decided what should come back.

eval_set = [
    {"query": "how does TLS handshake failure happen", "relevant_ids": {"doc_17", "doc_42"}},
    {"query": "password recovery steps", "relevant_ids": {"doc_3"}},
    # ... 30-100 labeled examples, more is better
]

def recall_at_k(collection, eval_set, k=5):
    hits = 0
    for example in eval_set:
        results = collection.query(query_texts=[example["query"]], n_results=k)
        returned_ids = set(results["ids"][0])
        if returned_ids & example["relevant_ids"]:
            hits += 1
    return hits / len(eval_set)

print("recall@5:", recall_at_k(collection, eval_set, k=5))

This version counts a query as a "hit" if any relevant document appears in the top-k — useful when one correct answer is enough. For queries with multiple relevant documents, you'll often also want a stricter metric:

def mean_recall_fraction_at_k(collection, eval_set, k=5):
    total = 0.0
    for example in eval_set:
        results = collection.query(query_texts=[example["query"]], n_results=k)
        returned_ids = set(results["ids"][0])
        relevant = example["relevant_ids"]
        total += len(returned_ids & relevant) / len(relevant)
    return total / len(eval_set)

This measures what fraction of all relevant documents you retrieved, not just whether you got at least one — important when a query genuinely has 3 correct documents and you only want credit for finding all of them.

docs.title: Measuring latency percentiles
docs.text:
Average latency hides the problem. If 99 queries take 10ms and 1 query takes 2 seconds, your average looks fine (~30ms) but one in a hundred users has a terrible experience. Percentiles expose this:

import time
import numpy as np

def measure_latency(collection, queries, n_results=5):
    timings = []
    for query in queries:
        start = time.perf_counter()
        collection.query(query_texts=[query], n_results=n_results)
        timings.append((time.perf_counter() - start) * 1000)  # ms

    timings = np.array(timings)
    return {
        "p50": float(np.percentile(timings, 50)),
        "p95": float(np.percentile(timings, 95)),
        "p99": float(np.percentile(timings, 99)),
        "max": float(timings.max()),
    }

print(measure_latency(collection, [e["query"] for e in eval_set] * 10))

p50 (median) tells you the typical experience. p95/p99 tell you the experience your worst-off users actually have — the numbers that matter for an SLA, because "average" latency is not what any individual slow request feels like.

docs.title: Load testing with concurrency
docs.text:
Single-threaded timing understates real-world latency, because production traffic is concurrent and a vector DB's index has shared resources (memory bandwidth, lock contention) that degrade under parallel load.

import concurrent.futures
import time

def load_test(collection, queries, concurrency=20, total_requests=200):
    def one_query(q):
        start = time.perf_counter()
        collection.query(query_texts=[q], n_results=5)
        return (time.perf_counter() - start) * 1000

    with concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=concurrency) as pool:
        work = [queries[i % len(queries)] for i in range(total_requests)]
        timings = list(pool.map(one_query, work))

    import numpy as np
    arr = np.array(timings)
    return {"p50": np.percentile(arr, 50), "p95": np.percentile(arr, 95), "p99": np.percentile(arr, 99)}

print(load_test(collection, [e["query"] for e in eval_set], concurrency=20, total_requests=200))

For a heavier, more realistic load test against an HTTP-based vector DB (Pinecone, Qdrant, Weaviate over their REST/gRPC APIs), a dedicated tool like locust lets you ramp concurrent users gradually and watch latency degrade as load increases, which a simple thread pool script won't show you as clearly.

docs.title: Tuning the recall/latency tradeoff
docs.text:
Most ANN indexes expose a runtime parameter that trades recall for latency directly:

  • HNSW: ef_search (sometimes called ef at query time) — how many candidate nodes to examine per layer during the graph traversal. Higher ef_search = better recall, higher latency.
  • IVF: nprobe — how many of the index's cluster partitions to search. Higher nprobe = better recall, higher latency, same idea as ef_search.
# Qdrant example: raising ef_search at query time
client.query_points(
    collection_name="docs",
    query=query_vector,
    search_params={"hnsw_ef": 256},  # default is often 128; higher = more recall, slower
    limit=5,
)

The right value is whatever satisfies your latency budget while keeping recall@k above your quality bar on your eval set — there's no universally correct number, which is exactly why you benchmark both together rather than guessing one in isolation.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Build a 20-example eval set for your Chroma/Qdrant collection from earlier levels. Measure recall@5 and p50/p95/p99 latency at the index's default settings. Then raise the recall/latency tradeoff parameter (ef_search or equivalent) and re-measure both. Plot or tabulate how recall and p95 latency move together as you increase it — find the point of diminishing returns where more latency stops buying meaningfully better recall.

docs.title: What's worth caching in a RAG pipeline
docs.text: A typical query touches several expensive steps: embed the query (a model forward pass), search the vector DB (an ANN traversal), sometimes re-rank (another model forward pass), and often call an LLM with the retrieved context (the most expensive step of all). Caching at any of these layers avoids redoing work that's likely to repeat — and in most real traffic, query repetition is much higher than people expect (common questions, retry clicks, near-duplicate phrasing).

docs.title: Exact-match query caching
docs.text:
The simplest cache: hash the normalized query text and cache the full result.

import hashlib
import json

class ExactQueryCache:
    def __init__(self):
        self._store = {}

    def _key(self, query: str) -> str:
        normalized = query.strip().lower()
        return hashlib.sha256(normalized.encode()).hexdigest()

    def get(self, query: str):
        return self._store.get(self._key(query))

    def set(self, query: str, result):
        self._store[self._key(query)] = result

cache = ExactQueryCache()

def cached_search(collection, query, n_results=5):
    if hit := cache.get(query):
        return hit
    result = collection.query(query_texts=[query], n_results=n_results)
    cache.set(query, result)
    return result

For production, back this with Redis (SETEX with a TTL) instead of an in-memory dict, so the cache survives restarts and is shared across multiple app instances:

import redis
import json

r = redis.Redis(host="localhost", port=6379)

def cached_search_redis(collection, query, n_results=5, ttl_seconds=3600):
    key = "qcache:" + hashlib.sha256(query.strip().lower().encode()).hexdigest()
    if cached := r.get(key):
        return json.loads(cached)
    result = collection.query(query_texts=[query], n_results=n_results)
    r.setex(key, ttl_seconds, json.dumps(result))
    return result

Exact-match caching catches identical repeat queries but misses the far more common case: the same intent, worded slightly differently ("reset my password" vs. "how do I reset my password" vs. "password reset steps").

docs.title: Semantic caching
docs.text:
A semantic cache stores past queries' embeddings alongside their results, and on a new query, checks whether any cached query is similar enough (above a similarity threshold) to reuse.

import numpy as np

class SemanticCache:
    def __init__(self, model, threshold: float = 0.95):
        self.model = model
        self.threshold = threshold
        self.entries = []  # list of (embedding, query_text, result)

    def get(self, query: str):
        if not self.entries:
            return None
        q_emb = self.model.encode([query], normalize_embeddings=True)[0]
        sims = [float(q_emb @ e[0]) for e in self.entries]
        best_idx = int(np.argmax(sims))
        if sims[best_idx] >= self.threshold:
            return self.entries[best_idx][2]
        return None

    def set(self, query: str, result):
        q_emb = self.model.encode([query], normalize_embeddings=True)[0]
        self.entries.append((q_emb, query, result))

semantic_cache = SemanticCache(model, threshold=0.95)

def cached_search_semantic(collection, query, n_results=5):
    if hit := semantic_cache.get(query):
        return hit
    result = collection.query(query_texts=[query], n_results=n_results)
    semantic_cache.set(query, result)
    return result

The threshold matters a lot: too low (e.g. 0.80) and you'll serve a cached answer for a genuinely different question; too high (e.g. 0.99) and you'll rarely get a cache hit at all. 0.92-0.97 is a common practical range for all-MiniLM-L6-v2-style models, but always tune it against your own eval set rather than trusting a default — "close enough" is domain-specific.

Note the cost tradeoff: a semantic cache check itself requires computing the query embedding, so it only pays off when it saves something more expensive than that (the vector DB search, re-ranking, or an LLM call) — it isn't free, it's cheaper-than-the-alternative.

docs.title: Embedding caching
docs.text:
If the same piece of text gets embedded repeatedly — common with chunk re-indexing jobs, or user-facing autocomplete that re-embeds partial queries — cache the embedding itself, keyed by the exact text:

from functools import lru_cache

@lru_cache(maxsize=10_000)
def embed_cached(text: str) -> tuple:
    return tuple(model.encode([text], normalize_embeddings=True)[0])

lru_cache is process-local and fine for a single service instance; for multi-instance deployments, the same Redis pattern as above works — embcache:<sha256 of text> → the embedding bytes.

docs.title: Connection pooling and batching
docs.text:
Two more latency wins that aren't about caching at all:

  • Connection pooling. Opening a new connection to a hosted vector DB (Pinecone, Qdrant Cloud) per request adds TCP/TLS handshake overhead on every call. Reuse a client instance across requests instead of constructing one per query — most client SDKs pool connections automatically if you reuse the client object.
  • Batching. If your application needs to embed or query many items at once (e.g. re-indexing, or a bulk recommendation job), batch them into one encode()/query() call instead of looping one at a time. A model forward pass over a batch of 32 is dramatically faster per-item than 32 separate forward passes, because it better utilizes the hardware (CPU vectorization or GPU parallelism) in one shot.
# Slow: one embedding call per text
embeddings = [model.encode([t])[0] for t in texts]

# Fast: one batched call for all texts
embeddings = model.encode(texts, batch_size=32)

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Add a semantic cache in front of your search function from earlier levels. Run a batch of 20 queries where some are near-paraphrases of each other (e.g. "how do I reset my password" and "steps to recover my account login"). Measure the cache hit rate at threshold 0.90 vs 0.97, and check whether any hits at the lower threshold returned results for a genuinely different question — that's your signal for where the threshold needs to sit for your own data.

docs.title: What breaks silently in production
docs.text: A vector search system doesn't throw errors when it's returning mediocre results — it just... returns mediocre results. Unlike a crashed API call, degraded retrieval quality produces no exception, no 500 status code, nothing in your error logs. You find out from a frustrated user, or you don't find out at all. Observability here means deliberately watching things that don't announce themselves.

docs.title: What to monitor
docs.text:
• Query latency (p50/p95/p99, per the previous lesson) — watch for gradual creep as your index grows, not just hard failures.
  • Error rates — timeouts, connection failures, malformed queries (empty strings, queries exceeding a model's max token length).
  • Index size and memory — HNSW graphs and IVF indexes grow with your corpus; watch memory usage so you catch an approaching capacity ceiling before it causes an outage, not after.
  • Recall drift — the quality metric from lesson 5, measured repeatedly over time, not just once at launch. A corpus that grows, an embedding model that gets silently upgraded by a hosted API, or a shift in the kind of questions users ask can all erode recall without any infrastructure alarm going off.
  • Zero-result and low-confidence-result rates — queries where the top result's similarity score is below a sane threshold are a proxy for "the system had nothing good to say," worth tracking as its own rate over time.

docs.title: Structured logging for offline analysis
docs.text:
Log every query with enough structure to analyze later — not just "query succeeded", but what was asked, what came back, and how confident the system was:

import logging
import json
import time

logger = logging.getLogger("vector_search")

def logged_search(collection, query, n_results=5):
    start = time.perf_counter()
    result = collection.query(query_texts=[query], n_results=n_results)
    latency_ms = (time.perf_counter() - start) * 1000

    distances = result.get("distances", [[]])[0]
    log_entry = {
        "query": query,
        "n_results": n_results,
        "returned_ids": result["ids"][0],
        "top_distance": distances[0] if distances else None,
        "latency_ms": round(latency_ms, 2),
        "timestamp": time.time(),
    }
    logger.info(json.dumps(log_entry))
    return result

Structured (JSON) logs like this can be shipped to any log aggregation system (Elasticsearch, Datadog, CloudWatch Logs Insights) and queried later: "show me all queries from the last week with top_distance below 0.3" is exactly the kind of offline analysis that catches a retrieval quality problem your dashboards never surfaced as an alert.

docs.title: Metrics instrumentation with Prometheus
docs.text:
Logs are good for forensic analysis of individual queries; metrics are good for dashboards and alerting on aggregate trends.

pip install prometheus-client

from prometheus_client import Histogram, Counter, start_http_server

SEARCH_LATENCY = Histogram(
    "vector_search_latency_seconds",
    "Time spent on vector search queries",
    buckets=[0.005, 0.01, 0.025, 0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0],
)
SEARCH_ERRORS = Counter("vector_search_errors_total", "Failed vector search queries")
LOW_CONFIDENCE_RESULTS = Counter(
    "vector_search_low_confidence_total",
    "Queries whose top result fell below the confidence threshold",
)

def instrumented_search(collection, query, n_results=5, confidence_threshold=0.3):
    with SEARCH_LATENCY.time():
        try:
            result = collection.query(query_texts=[query], n_results=n_results)
        except Exception:
            SEARCH_ERRORS.inc()
            raise

    distances = result.get("distances", [[]])[0]
    if distances and distances[0] > confidence_threshold:
        LOW_CONFIDENCE_RESULTS.inc()
    return result

start_http_server(8000)  # Prometheus scrapes metrics from :8000/metrics

With this running, a Grafana dashboard can plot p95 latency, error rate, and the low-confidence-result rate over time — and you can alert when any of them crosses a threshold, turning "silent degradation" into "a page at 2am," which, perhaps counterintuitively, is exactly the improvement you want.

docs.title: Scheduled recall re-measurement
docs.text:
The single most important observability practice for retrieval quality specifically: don't just measure recall@k once at launch — re-run your eval set on a schedule (nightly, or on every deploy) and track the trend.

# A simple scheduled job (run via cron, Airflow, or a CI pipeline)
def nightly_recall_check(collection, eval_set, alert_threshold=0.85):
    score = recall_at_k(collection, eval_set, k=5)  # from lesson 5
    logger.info(json.dumps({"metric": "nightly_recall_at_5", "value": score, "timestamp": time.time()}))
    if score < alert_threshold:
        # page someone, post to Slack, whatever your alerting path is
        raise RuntimeError(f"Recall@5 dropped to {score:.3f}, below threshold {alert_threshold}")

This is the only reliable way to catch the scenario from the top of this lesson: a corpus growing in a way that dilutes relevance, or an upstream embedding API quietly changing, before a human notices the symptoms.

Run 50 varied queries through it, including a few you expect to have no good answer in your corpus, and inspect /metrics to confirm the histogram and counters populated as expected. Then write the nightly_recall_check function against your eval set from lesson 5 and confirm it raises when you artificially lower the threshold above your current score.

docs.title: Updates are re-embed-and-upsert
docs.text:
Unlike a traditional database row, you can't "edit a vector" in place when the underlying text changes — the embedding is a function of the text, so a changed document needs a freshly computed embedding. The pattern is always: re-embed the new text, then upsert (update-or-insert) by a stable ID.

def update_document(collection, doc_id: str, new_text: str, metadata: dict | None = None):
    new_embedding = model.encode([new_text], normalize_embeddings=True)[0].tolist()
    collection.upsert(
        ids=[doc_id],
        embeddings=[new_embedding],
        documents=[new_text],
        metadatas=[metadata or {}],
    )

The critical design decision this depends on: every document needs a stable, deterministic ID that doesn't change when its content does — a database primary key, a content hash of a stable identifier (not of the text itself, which changes), or a URL/path. If you don't have a stable ID scheme, "updating" a document actually means deleting the old one with a different embedding and never actually replacing it — a silent duplicate bug that's easy to miss until your corpus mysteriously doubles in size.

docs.title: Soft delete vs. hard delete
docs.text:
• Hard delete removes the vector and all its metadata immediately and irreversibly — collection.delete(ids=["doc_42"]). Simple, but there's no undo, and in distributed systems it may take a moment to propagate (see consistency below).
  • Soft delete marks a document as deleted via metadata instead of removing it, and filters it out at query time:
def soft_delete(collection, doc_id: str):
    collection.update(ids=[doc_id], metadatas=[{"deleted": True}])

def search_excluding_deleted(collection, query, n_results=5):
    return collection.query(
        query_texts=[query],
        n_results=n_results,
        where={"deleted": {"$ne": True}},
    )

Soft delete is reversible (undelete is just flipping the flag back) and preserves an audit trail, but it means every query needs the exclusion filter, and the "deleted" vectors still consume index space and memory until a background job actually purges them. Most production systems that need compliance/audit trails use soft delete with a periodic hard-delete sweep for anything soft-deleted past a retention window.

docs.title: Eventual consistency in distributed vector databases
docs.text:
Managed, horizontally-scaled vector databases (Pinecone, Weaviate Cloud, distributed Qdrant clusters) typically replicate data across multiple nodes for availability. A write (insert/update/delete) has to propagate to those replicas, and — depending on the database's consistency model — a query that lands on a replica that hasn't yet received the latest write can return stale results for a short window after the write.

# This sequence can genuinely return the deleted document in some systems
collection.delete(ids=["doc_42"])
results = collection.query(query_texts=["some query"], n_results=5)
# doc_42 might still appear here for a brief period — not a bug, it's propagation lag

This is called eventual consistency: the system guarantees that, given enough time with no further writes, all replicas converge to the same state — but it does not guarantee a read immediately after a write reflects that write everywhere. If your application has a hard requirement that a delete must be invisible to the very next read (e.g. "right to be forgotten" compliance), check your specific vector DB's consistency guarantees and available options — some offer a "strong consistency" read mode at a latency cost, used selectively rather than by default.

docs.title: Re-indexing when the embedding model changes
docs.text:
Swapping embedding models (upgrading to a better one, or switching providers) is not a metadata update — every existing vector was produced by the old model's weights, and the new model's vector space is not comparable to the old one at all. A cosine similarity between an old-model-embedded query and a new-model-embedded document is meaningless.

def reindex_with_new_model(old_collection, new_collection, new_model, batch_size=256):
    offset = 0
    while True:
        batch = old_collection.get(limit=batch_size, offset=offset, include=["documents", "metadatas"])
        if not batch["ids"]:
            break
        new_embeddings = new_model.encode(batch["documents"], normalize_embeddings=True).tolist()
        new_collection.upsert(
            ids=batch["ids"],
            embeddings=new_embeddings,
            documents=batch["documents"],
            metadatas=batch["metadatas"],
        )
        offset += batch_size

The safe rollout pattern: build the new collection fully in parallel (as above), validate it (recall@k against your eval set, lesson 5) before cutting traffic over, then switch your application's reads to the new collection — and only delete the old one once you're confident, giving yourself a rollback path if the new model underperforms in ways your eval set didn't catch.

docs.title: What actually drives vector DB cost
docs.text:
At meaningful scale (tens of millions of vectors and up), cost comes from a few distinct places, and they don't all respond to the same fix:

  • Storage — raw vector bytes, plus index overhead (HNSW graphs typically add 20-50% on top of raw vector storage for the graph edges), plus metadata.
  • Write/compute operations — inserts, upserts, and deletes, especially on managed/serverless pricing where each operation has a cost.
  • Query operations — each search call, sometimes billed per-query, sometimes bundled into compute-time pricing.
  • Embedding generation — if you use a hosted embedding API rather than a local model, every document (and every query) you embed is a metered API call, and for a large or frequently re-indexed corpus this can dwarf the vector DB's own bill.

docs.title: Serverless vs. reserved/dedicated pricing
docs.text:
Most managed vector DBs (Pinecone, Qdrant Cloud, Weaviate Cloud) offer both:

  • Serverless — pay per operation and per GB stored, no idle capacity to provision. Cost scales directly with usage, which is cheap at low/bursty volume but can get expensive per-unit at sustained high volume.
  • Reserved/dedicated — pay a fixed rate for provisioned compute/memory regardless of how much you actually use. Cheaper per-unit at high, steady volume, but you're paying for idle capacity during quiet periods.

The crossover point is a function of your actual query/write volume and how steady it is — a workload with predictable, high, constant traffic usually favors reserved; a spiky or low-volume workload usually favors serverless. The only reliable way to know which is cheaper for you is to estimate both against your real (or realistically projected) traffic, not a vendor's example numbers.

docs.title: Dimensionality reduction
docs.text:
A smaller embedding dimension means less storage per vector and faster distance computation (fewer multiply-adds per comparison), at some cost to representational quality.

from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
import numpy as np

# Reduce 768-dim embeddings to 256-dim, fit on a representative sample
pca = PCA(n_components=256)
reduced_sample = pca.fit(sample_embeddings)  # fit once on a large enough sample

def reduce_embedding(full_embedding: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    reduced = pca.transform([full_embedding])[0]
    return reduced / np.linalg.norm(reduced)  # re-normalize after reduction

Some embedding models are explicitly trained to support this natively — Matryoshka embeddings (covered in the next lesson) produce vectors where the first N dimensions are already a valid, independently useful lower-dimensional embedding, so you can truncate instead of needing a separate PCA step.

docs.title: Quantization
docs.text:
Quantization reduces the precision of each number in a vector rather than the count of numbers — storing each dimension in fewer bits.

  • Float32 → int8 (scalar quantization): roughly 4x storage reduction. Each dimension is mapped from its float range into 256 discrete levels. Recall impact is typically small (often under 1-2 percentage points) if done carefully with a calibrated range.
  • Binary quantization: each dimension becomes a single bit (sign only). This is roughly 32x storage reduction compared to float32, with a larger recall hit, but is fast enough to use as a cheap first-pass filter before a more precise re-scoring step on the original float vectors.
def quantize_int8(vector: np.ndarray, vmin: float, vmax: float) -> np.ndarray:
    scale = 255.0 / (vmax - vmin)
    return np.clip(((vector - vmin) * scale), 0, 255).astype(np.uint8)

Most managed vector databases (Qdrant, Weaviate) support quantization as a built-in index option rather than requiring you to hand-roll it — the pattern above is to understand the mechanism, not to reimplement it in production.

docs.title: Caching to cut embedding-API spend
docs.text:
If you're embedding with a hosted API (rather than a free local model), every repeat or near-duplicate text you re-embed is paying twice for the same work. The embedding cache from lesson 6 (lru_cache or Redis, keyed by exact text) directly reduces this cost line — and for corpora with a lot of near-duplicate content (templated documents, boilerplate sections repeated across many files), de-duplicating identical chunks before embedding at all is often the single biggest lever:

def dedupe_before_embedding(chunks: list[str]) -> tuple[list[str], dict[int, int]]:
    """Returns unique chunks plus a mapping from original index to unique index."""
    seen: dict[str, int] = {}
    unique_chunks = []
    index_map = {}
    for i, chunk in enumerate(chunks):
        if chunk not in seen:
            seen[chunk] = len(unique_chunks)
            unique_chunks.append(chunk)
        index_map[i] = seen[chunk]
    return unique_chunks, index_map

Then measure recall@5 (from lesson 5) on both — the full-precision version and a simulated int8-quantized version using the quantize_int8 function above (quantize, then dequantize back to float before comparing, to simulate the precision loss) — and report how much recall you actually lose for the storage savings.

docs.title: 10 · Project — Benchmark & Optimize a RAG Pipeline
The goal
docs.text:
Everything in this level is a tool for answering one question: did my change actually make retrieval better, and at what latency cost? This project makes you answer that question for real, on your own pipeline, instead of taking it on faith that hybrid search or re-ranking "should" help.

You'll take the retrieval service you built in Level 2 (or a similar multi-document Chroma/Qdrant setup if you skipped straight here), build a small labeled eval set, measure its baseline quality and speed, apply at least two improvements from this level, and measure the delta.

docs.title: Step 1 — Build a labeled eval set
docs.text:
You need 20-50 (query, relevant_doc_ids) pairs, grounded in documents that actually exist in your corpus. If you don't have real user queries to draw from yet, write them yourself: pick a document, write a question that document specifically and uniquely answers, record its ID as the answer.

eval_set = [
    {"query": "...", "relevant_ids": {"doc_17"}},
    # ... 20-50 total, covering a mix of exact-term queries and paraphrased ones
]

Deliberately include a few queries that contain exact identifiers (error codes, product names, specific numbers) — those are the ones hybrid search is supposed to help with, and you want your eval set capable of showing that.

docs.title: Step 2 — Measure the baseline
docs.text:
Reuse recall_at_k and measure_latency from lesson 5 against your current pipeline (dense vector search only, no re-ranking, no caching):

baseline_recall = recall_at_k(collection, eval_set, k=5)
baseline_latency = measure_latency(collection, [e["query"] for e in eval_set])

print("BASELINE")
print("recall@5:", baseline_recall)
print("latency:", baseline_latency)

Write these numbers down — literally save them to a file or print them somewhere you won't lose. Everything after this step is measured relative to this baseline.

docs.title: Step 3 — Apply at least two improvements
docs.text:
Pick at least two of the following (more is fine, but measure the effect of each addition, not just the final combination, so you know what actually contributed):

  • Hybrid search (lesson 1): add BM25 + RRF fusion alongside your existing dense retrieval.
  • Re-ranking (lesson 2): retrieve a wider candidate set and re-rank with a cross-encoder before returning the final top-k.
  • Better chunking (lesson 3): re-chunk your corpus with a sentence-aware or semantic strategy if you're currently using naive fixed-size chunks, and re-index.
  • Caching (lesson 6): add a semantic cache in front of search.
  • Index parameter tuning (lesson 5): raise ef_search/nprobe and measure the recall/latency tradeoff directly.

A good combination to demonstrate the clearest story: hybrid search + re-ranking, since the eval set's exact-term queries should show a visible recall jump specifically attributable to adding BM25, and the re-ranking step should show an improvement on the paraphrased queries — two different mechanisms, two different parts of your eval set responding to each.

def improved_search(query, collection, bm25, documents, top_k=5, retrieve_k=30):
    # Stage 1: hybrid retrieval (dense + sparse, fused with RRF)
    dense_ids = [doc_id for doc_id, _ in dense_search(query, top_k=retrieve_k)]
    sparse_ids = [doc_id for doc_id, _ in sparse_search(query, top_k=retrieve_k)]
    fused = rrf_fuse([dense_ids, sparse_ids])
    candidate_ids = [doc_id for doc_id, _ in fused[:retrieve_k]]
    candidates = [documents[i] for i in candidate_ids]

    # Stage 2: cross-encoder re-ranking down to the final top_k
    pairs = [[query, doc] for doc in candidates]
    scores = reranker.predict(pairs)
    ranked = sorted(zip(candidate_ids, candidates, scores), key=lambda t: -t[2])
    return ranked[:top_k]

docs.title: Step 4 — Measure the delta
docs.text:
Re-run the exact same recall_at_k and measure_latency measurements against the improved pipeline, on the exact same eval set:

improved_recall = recall_at_k_custom(improved_search, eval_set, k=5)  # adapt to your new function's signature
improved_latency = measure_latency_custom(improved_search, [e["query"] for e in eval_set])

print("IMPROVED")
print("recall@5:", improved_recall, " (baseline was", baseline_recall, ")")
print("latency:", improved_latency, " (baseline was", baseline_latency, ")")

Report both numbers honestly, including if latency got worse — re-ranking in particular will add latency (an extra model forward pass per candidate), and the real finding of this project is the tradeoff, not just "recall went up."

docs.title: Step 5 — Break it down by query type
docs.text:
The most informative analysis isn't the aggregate recall number — it's recall split by query type:

exact_term_queries = [e for e in eval_set if looks_like_exact_term(e["query"])]
paraphrase_queries = [e for e in eval_set if not looks_like_exact_term(e["query"])]

print("exact-term recall, baseline vs improved:",
      recall_at_k(collection, exact_term_queries, k=5), "vs",
      recall_at_k_custom(improved_search, exact_term_queries, k=5))

This is where you should see the clearest story: hybrid search should move the needle most on exact-term queries specifically, not uniformly across everything — if your results don't show that pattern, it's worth investigating why (a corpus too small to have real keyword-vs-paraphrase distinction, or an eval set that doesn't actually stress that difference).

docs.title: Deliverable
docs.text: A short write-up (a markdown file in your own notes, not part of this course) with: your baseline numbers, which improvements you added, the improved numbers, the recall/latency tradeoff you observed, and the query-type breakdown. This is the exact kind of before/after evidence a real team would want before shipping a retrieval change to production — which is the actual skill this project is teaching.

docs.text: Goal: design and operate complete, production-grade retrieval systems — architecture, evaluation, security, and the operational maturity a real platform needs.

By the end of this level you'll be able to architect, evaluate, secure, and operate a production retrieval system end to end — not just query a vector database, but own one in production.

docs.title: 01 · Advanced RAG Architectures
docs.text:
Everything so far has used the same shape: embed a query, fetch the top-k chunks, stuff them in a prompt, generate an answer. That's naive RAG, and it breaks down on questions that need more than one lookup, questions where the first retrieval misses because the query and the source text use different words, or questions that span multiple documents that never individually mention the full answer.

This lesson covers the architectures teams reach for when naive RAG stops being enough.

docs.title: Query rewriting and expansion
docs.text:
The user's literal query is often a bad search query. "What changed in the pricing model last quarter?" has no embedding neighbor in a doc that says "Q3 2025 subscription tier restructuring." A rewriting step uses an LLM to turn the user's question into one or more better search queries before anything touches the vector DB.

from openai import OpenAI  # any chat-completion client works here

client = OpenAI()

def rewrite_query(user_question: str, n: int = 3) -> list[str]:
    prompt = f"""Rewrite the following question as {n} different search
queries that would find relevant documents in a technical knowledge base.
Return one query per line, no numbering.

Question: {user_question}"""
    resp = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="gpt-4o-mini",
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
    )
    lines = resp.choices[0].message.content.strip().split("\n")
    return [l.strip() for l in lines if l.strip()]

queries = rewrite_query("What changed in the pricing model last quarter?")
# -> ["Q3 2025 pricing changes", "subscription tier restructuring 2025",
#     "pricing policy update history"]

Run each rewritten query through retrieval, merge and deduplicate the results (e.g. by chunk id, keeping the highest score seen), then proceed as normal. This alone fixes a large fraction of "the answer is in there but retrieval never found it" failures.

docs.title: Multi-hop retrieval
docs.text:
Some questions require chaining lookups: "Which vendor supplies the component that caused the Q2 outage?" needs you to first find what caused the Q2 outage, extract the component name, and then search for which vendor supplies it. A single retrieval pass can't do this because the second query doesn't exist until you've read the answer to the first.

A simple multi-hop loop:

def multi_hop_answer(question: str, retrieve, generate, max_hops: int = 3):
    context_chunks = []
    current_query = question

    for hop in range(max_hops):
        results = retrieve(current_query, top_k=5)
        context_chunks.extend(results)

        decision = generate(f"""Question: {question}
Context so far:
{format_chunks(context_chunks)}

Can you fully answer the question from this context? Reply YES or NO.
If NO, reply with a follow-up search query on a second line.""")

        if decision.startswith("YES"):
            break
        current_query = decision.split("\n")[-1].strip()

    return generate(f"""Question: {question}
Context:
{format_chunks(context_chunks)}

Answer the question using only the context above.""")

Each hop retrieves, checks whether it has enough to answer, and if not, generates the next query from what it just learned. This is strictly more expensive (multiple LLM calls, multiple retrievals per question) so it's worth gating: only run multi-hop for questions a cheap classifier flags as "probably needs more than one lookup."

docs.title: Agentic RAG
docs.text:
Query rewriting and multi-hop are both fixed patterns — a hardcoded loop shape. Agentic RAG goes further: the LLM is given retrieval as a tool it can call zero, one, or many times, in whatever order it decides, interleaved with reasoning.

tools = [{
    "type": "function",
    "function": {
        "name": "search_knowledge_base",
        "description": "Search the vector database for relevant document chunks.",
        "parameters": {
            "type": "object",
            "properties": {"query": {"type": "string"}},
            "required": ["query"],
        },
    },
}]

def agentic_rag(question: str, retrieve, client):
    messages = [{"role": "user", "content": question}]

    for _ in range(5):  # hard cap on tool-call rounds
        resp = client.chat.completions.create(
            model="gpt-4o", messages=messages, tools=tools,
        )
        msg = resp.choices[0].message
        messages.append(msg)

        if not msg.tool_calls:
            return msg.content  # model decided it has enough to answer

        for call in msg.tool_calls:
            query = json.loads(call.function.arguments)["query"]
            results = retrieve(query, top_k=5)
            messages.append({
                "role": "tool",
                "tool_call_id": call.id,
                "content": format_chunks(results),
            })

    return "Could not resolve within tool-call budget."

The model decides for itself: retrieve, decide it needs a different angle, retrieve again, or just answer directly if the question doesn't need retrieval at all (e.g. "summarize what you just told me"). This is the pattern behind most production "chat with your docs" agents today — multi-hop is really a special case of agentic RAG with the loop shape fixed in advance instead of left to the model.

docs.title: Graph-RAG, briefly
docs.text: Vector search finds chunks that are semantically similar to a query, but it's bad at questions about relationships: "which teams were affected by every incident that touched the auth service?" isn't a similarity question, it's a graph traversal. Graph-RAG systems extract entities and relationships from documents into a graph (often with an LLM doing extraction: "service X depends on service Y", "incident A affected team B") stored alongside the vector index. A query can then do both: traverse the graph for structural relationships, and fall back to vector search for anything the graph didn't capture. Building a full graph-RAG pipeline is out of scope here, but know the shape exists — when questions are fundamentally about connections between entities rather than similarity between text, a pure vector store is the wrong tool no matter how good your chunking is.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
1. Why rewriting helps more than better embedding models. Embedding models are trained to place paraphrases near each other, but a question and its answer are often not paraphrases of each other — "what changed" and "Q3 2025 restructuring" share no vocabulary and limited semantic overlap even though one answers the other. Rewriting closes this gap by using the LLM's world knowledge to guess vocabulary the source documents likely use, which is a different kind of signal than embedding similarity alone can provide.
  2. Why multi-hop needs a stopping condition, not a fixed hop count. Most questions resolve in one hop; forcing every question through three hops triples latency and cost for no benefit. The "can you answer yet?" check each round is what makes this adaptive instead of wasteful.
  3. Why agentic RAG can be worse than multi-hop on narrow domains. Giving the model full discretion over when to search means it can also decide not to search when it should have, hallucinating from parametric knowledge instead. Multi-hop's fixed loop is less flexible but more predictable — a reasonable default unless you've measured agentic RAG actually winning on your eval set (lesson 2 gives you the metrics to make that call with evidence instead of vibes).
  4. Where the cost actually goes. Every extra hop or tool call is a full LLM round trip, typically 1-3 seconds and real token cost. A naive RAG call might cost one generation; an agentic RAG call that takes 4 tool rounds costs five LLM calls. Architectures in this lesson trade latency and cost for correctness — always confirm the question mix in production actually needs it before deploying the more expensive pattern everywhere.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Take the multi_hop_answer function above and adapt it to run against your own retrieval setup (Chroma or whichever backend you've been using). Write three test questions: one that a single retrieval pass answers fine, one that genuinely needs two hops, and one that needs three. Log how many hops each one actually takes, and confirm the loop stops early on the easy question instead of always running to max_hops.

docs.title: 02 · Evaluating Retrieval Quality (Recall@K, MRR, NDCG)
docs.text: Every lesson so far has assumed retrieval works. It doesn't, automatically — chunking choices, embedding model choices, and index settings all change what comes back, often in ways that feel fine in a demo and fail silently in production. This lesson gives you the metrics to measure retrieval quality instead of eyeballing it, and a labeled eval set to measure it against.

docs.title: Building a labeled eval set
docs.text:
Before any metric means anything, you need queries with known-correct answers: for each query, which chunk ID(s) in your corpus should ideally come back.

eval_set = [
    {
        "query": "How do I reset a user's password via the admin API?",
        "relevant_chunk_ids": {"docs/admin-api.md#chunk-12"},
    },
    {
        "query": "What's the rate limit for the search endpoint?",
        "relevant_chunk_ids": {"docs/api-limits.md#chunk-3", "docs/api-limits.md#chunk-4"},
    },
    # 20-50 of these is a reasonable starting eval set
]

Label these by hand (or have domain experts label them) — this is the single highest-leverage thing you can do for retrieval quality, because every metric below is only as good as this ground truth.

docs.title: Recall@K
docs.text:
Recall@K asks: of all the relevant chunks that exist, what fraction did we get back in our top K results?

$$\text{Recall@K} = \frac{|\text{relevant} \cap \text{retrieved top-K}|}{|\text{relevant}|}$$

def recall_at_k(retrieved_ids: list[str], relevant_ids: set[str], k: int) -> float:
    top_k = set(retrieved_ids[:k])
    if not relevant_ids:
        return 0.0
    return len(top_k & relevant_ids) / len(relevant_ids)

retrieved = ["c3", "c12", "c7", "c4", "c9"]
relevant = {"c12", "c4"}
print(recall_at_k(retrieved, relevant, k=5))  # 1.0 — both relevant chunks are in top 5
print(recall_at_k(retrieved, relevant, k=2))  # 0.5 — only c12 is in top 2

Recall@K is the right metric when you care about completeness — e.g. a RAG system that needs every relevant chunk to answer a question fully, not just one.

docs.title: Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR)
docs.text:
MRR cares about how early the first relevant result appears, averaged across queries. It's the right metric when one good result is enough (e.g. "find the doc that answers this").

$$\text{RR} = \frac{1}{\text{rank of first relevant result}} \qquad \text{MRR} = \frac{1}{|Q|}\sum_{q \in Q} \text{RR}_q$$

def reciprocal_rank(retrieved_ids: list[str], relevant_ids: set[str]) -> float:
    for i, doc_id in enumerate(retrieved_ids, start=1):
        if doc_id in relevant_ids:
            return 1.0 / i
    return 0.0

def mrr(all_retrieved: list[list[str]], all_relevant: list[set[str]]) -> float:
    scores = [reciprocal_rank(r, rel) for r, rel in zip(all_retrieved, all_relevant)]
    return sum(scores) / len(scores)

# Worked example: first relevant chunk at rank 1, 3, and 2 across three queries
example_rrs = [1/1, 1/3, 1/2]
print(sum(example_rrs) / len(example_rrs))  # MRR = 0.611

A system that always puts the right answer first scores MRR = 1.0. One that puts it third on average scores MRR ≈ 0.33.

docs.title: NDCG (Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain)
docs.text:
NDCG handles graded relevance (not just relevant/irrelevant, but "this chunk is a perfect match," "this one is tangentially related") and rewards putting the best results earliest, with a logarithmic rank discount.

$$\text{DCG@K} = \sum_{i=1}^{K} \frac{2^{\text{rel}_i} - 1}{\log_2(i + 1)} \qquad \text{NDCG@K} = \frac{\text{DCG@K}}{\text{IDCG@K}}$$

where IDCG is the DCG of the ideal ordering (relevance scores sorted descending).

import math

def dcg_at_k(relevance_scores: list[int], k: int) -> float:
    return sum(
        (2**rel - 1) / math.log2(i + 2)
        for i, rel in enumerate(relevance_scores[:k])
    )

def ndcg_at_k(relevance_scores: list[int], k: int) -> float:
    ideal = sorted(relevance_scores, reverse=True)
    idcg = dcg_at_k(ideal, k)
    if idcg == 0:
        return 0.0
    return dcg_at_k(relevance_scores, k) / idcg

# Worked example: retrieved results have relevance grades 3, 0, 1, 2, 0
# (3 = perfect match, 0 = irrelevant)
scores = [3, 0, 1, 2, 0]
print(ndcg_at_k(scores, k=5))  # 0.869 — close to ideal, but the rank-2 miss costs us
print(ndcg_at_k(sorted(scores, reverse=True), k=5))  # 1.0 — ideal ordering by definition

docs.title: Which metric to use when
docs.text:
• Recall@K — you need all the relevant information (summarization, multi-fact answers, compliance-sensitive retrieval where missing a relevant doc is a real cost).
  • MRR — one good hit is enough and you care about how fast the user (or the LLM) finds it (FAQ search, "find me the doc").
  • NDCG — you have graded relevance judgments and care about the overall quality of the ranking, not just a binary hit/miss (search result pages, recommendation).

In practice, run all three against your labeled eval set whenever you change chunking, the embedding model, or index parameters (ef_search, nprobe, re-ranking) from earlier lessons — a change that looks neutral on one metric can be a regression on another, and only measuring tells you which.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
1. Why NDCG uses $2^{\text{rel}} - 1$ instead of just rel. The exponential gain function means a relevance-3 result is worth disproportionately more than three relevance-1 results — it models the intuition that one perfect answer beats several mediocre ones, which a linear scale would not capture.
  2. Why the log discount, not a linear one. $\log_2(i+1)$ penalizes rank 2 vs. rank 1 much more harshly (in relative terms) than it penalizes rank 20 vs. rank 19 — matching the real-world fact that users (and LLMs reading a limited context window) care enormously about the very top results and decreasingly about results far down the list.
  3. Why you normalize against the ideal DCG, not a fixed maximum. Two queries with different relevance-score distributions (one has five perfect matches available, another has only one) aren't directly comparable on raw DCG. Dividing by IDCG — the best possible DCG for that query's own ground truth — rescales every query to the same 0-1 range, so you can average NDCG across queries meaningfully.
  4. Why Recall@K can look great while users are unhappy. Recall@K only measures whether relevant chunks are somewhere in the top K — a system that recalls everything but buries the best chunk at rank 9 looks perfect on Recall@10 while being a poor experience if only the first 3 chunks fit in context. This is exactly the blind spot MRR and NDCG are built to catch, which is why production evals almost always report more than one metric side by side.
